# Free Lunch Lab

> Free Lunch Lab ("There is such a thing as a free lunch.") is a curated directory of apps and projects that pay you a basic income or rewards just for existing: crypto UBI, passive apps, cashback and more. Every entry links to its official source and has a "last checked" month, and the risks and cautions are listed next to the rewards. The site is available in 7 languages (en, ja, zh, hi, es, de, ar).

- Referral links: some sign-up links are the maintainer's referral links. They are marked in the data (`referral` in services.json) and labelled "Referral link" below; official URLs are always given too.
- License: content is CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), referral links excluded.
- Data last checked: 2026-11
- Short index: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/llms.txt

### Circles (Gnosis App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/circles/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Sign-up: invite only (needs an invitation, code or approval from an existing member)
- Verification: Web of trust / invites
- Trust check: Cash out: Unverified; Market price: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://app.gnosis.io/

A Gnosis project where every person issues their own currency. Circles 2.0 launched in May 2025, and in June 2026 the Gnosis App was rebuilt around Circles. This site has no referral link for it yet

What you get: 1 CRC per hour (24 per day)

What you need: Sign up in the Gnosis App and get invited by an existing Circles member. The inviter pays 96 CRC and the newcomer gets 48 CRC as a welcome bonus

Cautions: You can’t start without a member to invite you. CRC’s market price and ways to cash out are not confirmed. Gnosis has announced plans to spin the Gnosis App out of Gnosis Ltd into a separate company, so details may change

### Mercari

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/mercari/
- Category: Cashback sites
- Payout: one-time
- Region: Japan only
- Verification: Phone number, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://jp.mercari.com/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://link.jp.mercari.com/70tO/lpthbfqe
- Referral code (maintainer's own): AJVWZX

Mercari’s friend invite for its flea-market app. Sign up with an invite code and both you and the inviter get ¥500 in points (within 14 days). Turn on “Point Investment”, launched on Sept 15, 2026, and free points you receive automatically buy Bitcoin or Ethereum

What you get: ¥500 in points (can be auto-converted into Bitcoin and more)

What you need: Japan residents. Enter the invite code on the sign-up screen (it can’t be added later). Point Investment needs ID verification and age 18 to 74 (sign-up from Japan confirmed in Oct 2026)

Cautions: Points expire 30 days after you get them (counting that day). Point Investment only uses free points granted after you turn it on. There is no fee, but prices include a spread, and crypto can fall in value. Points obtained improperly are cancelled

Tap a button in the app once every 24 hours to earn PI. The more people you refer, the faster you mine. Opened to the public in February 2025 and trades on OKX, Bitget, MEXC and others

What you get: PI every day

What you need: Sign up via the invite link (invite code: eltociear). To move your PI you need identity verification and migration to the mainnet wallet

Cautions: The price is down about 97% from its 2025 high of $2.99 (about $0.08 as of October 2026). Not listed on Binance, Coinbase or Japanese exchanges. Needs a daily tap, so it won’t build up if you leave it alone

### Mein Grundeinkommen

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/meingrundeinkommen/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.mein-grundeinkommen.de/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://meinbge.de/fuer-dich/4143ce95b90cf10386f4?utm_campaign=freundschaft

A free lottery run by a nonprofit association in Berlin and funded by crowdfunding donations. Draws are held regularly, and each winner gets €1,000 a month for 12 months, no strings attached (real cash, not crypto)

What you get: €1,000 a month for a year if you win

What you need: Register with your email and confirm your participation for each draw. You must be 16 or older, and your name and date of birth must match your ID if you win

Cautions: A 2020 statement from the organisation said anyone can take part regardless of age or where they live, but current rules for people outside Germany and payouts abroad are not confirmed. The site is in German. It's a lottery, so most entrants receive nothing. Winnings may be taxed in your country

### UBI4ALL

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/ubi4all/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification, ID document KYC (optional)
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.ubi4all.org/

A free raffle run by a German non-profit. Each time donations reach €9,600, a basic income worth €9,600 in total is raffled off, paid in cash with no strings attached. High-income countries such as Japan get €800 a month for 1 year, low-income countries €160 a month for 5 years. No referral bonus

What you get: €9,600 if you win (in Japan: €800 a month for a year)

What you need: Create a free account on the official site and register for each raffle (monthly donors from €1 are entered automatically). You must be 16 or older, and winners are verified with ID. Sign-up from Japan has not yet been tested by this site

Cautions: It’s a raffle, so the odds are low and depend on how many people take part. Raffles only happen when donations fill the €9,600 pot, so the timing is irregular. Unless you are a UBI Beaver, you have to register for each raffle. Residents of the previous winner’s country are excluded from the next draw. Payouts go to SEPA bank accounts; other methods have their fees taken from the prize. How the prize is taxed depends on your country

### Ğ1 (June)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/g1/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Sign-up: invite only (needs an invitation, code or approval from an existing member)
- Verification: Web of trust / invites
- Trust check: Cash out: With conditions; Market price: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://duniter.org/g1/

A libre currency based on the Relative Theory of Money. It runs on the open-source Duniter software, and every member receives newly created Ğ1 each day as a “Universal Dividend”. Launched in March 2017 and moved to Duniter v2 in March 2026. There is no referral link or referral bonus

What you get: Ğ1 every day once you are a member (Universal Dividend)

What you need: Create a wallet and get certified by at least 5 existing members through the Web of Trust. Certifiers are expected to know you in person

Cautions: The community is mostly French-speaking and built on in-person ties, so joining from outside it (e.g. from Japan) is very hard. Non-members can still hold Ğ1 in a wallet but do not receive the daily dividend. Ğ1 is mainly traded for goods and services, and swapping it for regular money is peer-to-peer only

### Palai

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/palai/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: Phone number
- Trust check: Cash out: No; Public operator: Unverified
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://palai.org/en
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://palai.org/en?referrer=eltociear%2B856536b6d-da3a-4f27-9bcf-8eef2ce05bc2

A currency that pays everyone a daily basic income just for being human. No app to install and nothing to pay. Unspent balances slowly “evaporate”, and that amount is redistributed as basic income. Refer a friend and you get one extra day of basic income

What you get: Palai (¶) basic income every day

What you need: Sign up via the referral link and get certified by adding a mobile phone number (no ID needed). You claim your income yourself; days not claimed within 10 days are lost

Cautions: As of Oct 2026 there is no way to cash Palai out into euros or other money and no official exchange rate; you can only trade it for goods and services with people who accept Palai. The site doesn’t name the operator, only that it is “supported by Social Impact Lab Leipzig”

### Dotare

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/dotare/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: not specified
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://dotare.io/

A global basic income fund on Cardano. Donated ADA is put to work through staking and similar, and the earnings are paid to recipients in ADA each month. For 2027 that is 10 ADA a month for 12 months. No income test. Run by Dotare, LLC in the US. No referral bonus

What you get: 10 ADA a month for a year if you are chosen (2027 cycle)

What you need: Be 18 or older. Sign up on the official site and apply for each year you want to take part. When your turn comes, pass a quick identity check (to show you are human) and set up a Cardano wallet to receive payments

Cautions: For the 2027 cycle, applications closed on 31 Aug 2026 and enrollment closes on 30 Nov 2026; when someone signing up now would start receiving is not confirmed. Payouts go in line order, and as of 24 Oct 2026 the site showed 147 citizens and 2 beneficiaries. ADA’s price swings a lot

A mini app inside World App that lets you claim the World Chain token ORO once a day. World’s listing says inviting friends earns more ORO, but as of Oct 2026 we found no invite link in the app. Developed by Grupo de Fiesta

What you get: ORO tokens every day

What you need: Install World App, prove you are human with World ID (confirmed from Japan with Orb verification), then open the ORO mini app and claim every day

Cautions: The daily amount is not stated officially. It is unknown whether a verification level below Orb is enough. ORO trades on DEXs but liquidity is small, and 1 ORO is worth less than ¥1 (Oct 2026). No company information about the operator could be found

### AXO (World App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/axo/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: World ID (Orb)

- Referral code (maintainer's own): 932BDA

A mini app inside World App: tap once a day to claim the World Chain token AXO. The “Premium” plan (1 WLD a month) triples the daily amount. There is also a referral system. The founder is David Mateos

What you get: AXO tokens every day

AXO can be swapped for WLD on a decentralized exchange (DEX), but as of Oct 2026 liquidity is only about $2,000 and one AXO is worth a tiny fraction of a cent. No operating company details were found

### AI-DAC (World App)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/aidac/
- Category: Crypto basic income
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: World ID (Orb)
- Trust check: Cash out: With conditions; Market price: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://lp.ai-dac.com/

A mini app inside World App that calls itself an “AI-powered universal basic income platform”. People verified as human with World ID receive DAC and use it to back autonomous “AI CEOs” that build apps, and to vote on releases. Run by its founder, Kei Iwami. No referral bonus

What you get: UBI in DAC tokens

What you need: Open the AI-DAC mini app in World App and prove you are human with World ID (confirmed from Japan with Orb verification)

Cautions: The amount, frequency and how to cash out are not stated officially. It is unknown whether a verification level below Orb is enough. DAC has no supply cap: the operator can mint more at any time, which can dilute its value. The official site says its value is not guaranteed, and DEX liquidity is tiny (Oct 2026)

### Ubiquitus

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/ubiquitus/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: US residents only, not available from Japan
- Verification: not specified
- Trust check: Cash out: Yes; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://www.ubiquitus.org/

A US social experiment in a “basic income anyone can join”. Donations go into an invested fund, and each month 0.5% of it is split equally among all participants and paid via Venmo. Donating does not increase what you get. Founded by Ryan Frigo. No referral bonus

What you get: A small equal cash share on the 1st of each month (Venmo)

What you need: US residents aged 18+. Verify with a 1¢ Venmo transaction (no ID upload, no means test)

Cautions: As of Oct 2026 it cannot be used from Japan (the terms limit it to US residents; not working from Japan was confirmed first-hand). The per-person amount is tiny, falls with the pool, and payouts are stated to be not guaranteed and able to stop at any time. It describes itself as an informal social experiment, not a company. Recipients must report payments as income

### Gradido

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/services/gradido/
- Category: Passive apps
- Payout: recurring
- Region: available in Japan and worldwide
- Verification: No verification
- Trust check: Cash out: Unverified; Public operator: Yes
- Last checked: 2026-10
- Official URL: https://gradido.net/en/
- Referral link (maintainer's own referral; not covered by the content license): https://gdd.gradido.net/u/eltociear

A currency system that calls itself a “natural economy”. Work for the common good earns an “active basic income” of 20 GDD an hour, up to 1,000 GDD a month. Unspent money shrinks at 50% a year. Run by Gradido Akademie in Austria

What you get: 20 GDD per hour of common-good work (up to 1,000 GDD a month)

What you need: Create a free Gradido account through the referral link, record your contributions to the common good and receive GDD (tested first-hand from Japan in Oct 2026)

Cautions: The official FAQ says it is for now a “gratitude points reward system”, not a cryptocurrency. There is no official way stated to exchange GDD for euros or other money. If someone you referred later contributes money (e.g. a donation), you receive GDT; signing up alone earns nothing

## Essays

### Has generative AI taken our jobs? The data, and what basic income can do (Part 1)

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/generative-ai-jobs-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-07

On 5 November 2026 the US outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas published its monthly count of announced job cuts. From January to October 2026, employers cited artificial intelligence as the reason for 121,401 cuts, about 20% of the 617,189 total. Since the firm began tracking that reason in 2023, the count has reached 193,226.[1]

Numbers like these feed a familiar story: generative AI is taking jobs, and fast. This site supports basic income, and AI is one of the reasons people most often give for it. That is exactly why we wanted to know what has actually been measured before asking what a basic income could do. This is part 1 of two. It looks at jobs in general; part 2 will look at creative work.

#### What the 121,401 does and does not mean

Challenger counts the reasons employers give when they announce cuts. It does not measure how many jobs AI actually did away with. In October 2026, AI was cited for only 1,265 cuts, the lowest month of the year, and “market/economic conditions” (130,531) has overtaken AI as the top reason for the year so far.[1]

Some economists suspect that part of the AI figure is window dressing. In a January 2026 briefing, Oxford Economics noted that AI had been cited for nearly 55,000 US cuts in the first 11 months of 2025, just 4.5% of the total, and wrote: “We suspect some firms are trying to dress up layoffs as a good news story rather than bad news, such as past over-hiring.”[2] Telling investors that a smaller team is the fruit of AI sounds better than admitting to having hired too many people.

Opinion: An announced reason is a statement, not a measurement. To see what AI has done to jobs, we have to look at labour-market data.

#### The big picture: no clear footprint yet

The Budget Lab at Yale tracks the US labour market for signs of AI. Its September 2026 update, using data through August, says the analysis “does not yet clearly indicate an AI-related labor market footprint” and that “measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment.”[3]

Denmark offers a tighter test. Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard linked surveys of AI use in 11 exposed occupations to the country’s administrative records. In the revised version of their paper (March 2026), they rule out effects on earnings or recorded hours larger than 2% two years after ChatGPT’s launch.[4]

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr put it plainly in February 2026: “AI has yet to have a substantial effect on aggregate employment or unemployment.”[5] Economists at the Dallas Fed did the arithmetic. The share of 20- to 24-year-olds working in the most AI-exposed occupations fell from 16.4% in November 2022 to 15.5% in September 2025. Even if all of that had turned into unemployment, it would have added only about 0.1 point to the national rate.[6]

Opinion: For the labour market as a whole, “AI is taking jobs” is not yet visible in the data.

#### But the entry door is narrowing

That is not the end of the story. Look at who is not being hired, rather than who is being let go, and a consistent signal appears.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen at Stanford use payroll records from ADP, the largest US payroll processor. In their revised paper of August 2026, with data through June 2026, employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, such as software development and customer service, is about 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with people of the same age in less-exposed jobs. Earlier versions of the paper put the gap at 13% and then 15%; it has widened as more data came in. Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable gap. The authors stress that these are “descriptive patterns, not causal estimates”.[7]

Other studies, using other data, point the same way. A King’s College London study of UK firms found that highly exposed firms cut total employment by 4.5% on average, with junior positions down 5.8%, almost the whole decline; they were also 16.3 percentage points less likely to post new vacancies.[8] Two US Census Bureau working papers found that early-career employment in the most AI-exposed fifth of industries fell 12% over the ten quarters after ChatGPT. Graduates of the most exposed tenth of college majors became 5 percentage points less likely to have a job a quarter after graduating, and their starting earnings fell 13%, roughly what economists would expect from graduating into a severe recession.[9] Anthropic, the company behind the AI model Claude, found no systematic rise in unemployment among highly exposed workers, but a job-finding rate for 22- to 25-year-olds entering the most exposed jobs about 14% below 2022, a result it calls barely significant.[10]

What these studies share is the mechanism. The fall comes mainly from fewer young people being hired, not from more people being dismissed.[6][7][9] Firms keep the staff they have and quietly stop filling the bottom rung. The Census papers also find that hiring had largely recovered by early 2025, but from a smaller base: the door reopened only part of the way.[9]

Opinion: AI’s first visible effect is not mass layoffs but a narrower entrance. It is easy to miss, because a job that was never offered never shows up as a job lost.

#### Freelancers felt it first

The other place the effect shows clearly is in markets where work is bought task by task. Xiang Hui, Oren Reshef and Luofeng Zhou studied the freelance platform Upwork. After ChatGPT’s release, writing-related freelancers saw their monthly jobs fall 2% and their monthly earnings fall 5.2%. After the image generators DALL-E 2 and Midjourney, image-related freelancers lost 3.7% of their jobs and 9.4% of their earnings.[11]

Freelancers have no employer to keep them on, no notice period and, in many countries, little or no unemployment insurance. When a client switches to a tool, the income simply stops. Part 2 will look at creative work more closely.

The main studies side by side:

| Study | Data | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yale Budget Lab | US labour-force survey, to Aug 2026 | No clear AI footprint on employment or unemployment[3] |
| Humlum & Vestergaard | Danish administrative records | Effects on earnings and hours above 2% ruled out[4] |
| Brynjolfsson, Chandar & Chen (Stanford) | ADP payroll, to Jun 2026 | Ages 22–25 in the most exposed jobs: about 19% below trend (revised figure)[7] |
| King’s College London | UK job postings and profiles | Exposed firms: junior roles −5.8%[8] |
| US Census Bureau | US administrative records | Early-career jobs in the most exposed industries −12%; starting pay for the most exposed majors −13%[9] |
| Anthropic | US labour-force survey | No systematic rise in unemployment; young job-finding rate about −14%[10] |
| Hui, Reshef & Zhou | Upwork | Writing: jobs −2%, earnings −5.2%; images: −3.7%, −9.4%[11] |

#### When companies say AI was the reason

Some companies have said plainly that AI is why they need fewer people. In February 2026 Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, cut more than 4,000 of its more than 10,000 staff. The shareholder letter said: “Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company,” and “A significantly smaller team, using the tools we’re building, can do more and do it better.” Block’s fourth-quarter gross profit was up 24% on a year earlier: this was a company cutting while doing well, not one in trouble.[12] In September 2025 Salesforce’s chief executive Marc Benioff said he had cut support staff “from 9,000 heads to about 5,000, because I need less heads”, with half of customer conversations now handled by AI agents.[13]

Surveys of firms show how unusual these cases still are. In the New York Fed’s 2026 regional business surveys, 61% of service firms had used AI in the past six months, but only 4% reported AI-driven layoffs. About 15% said they had hired fewer people because of AI, and about 13% said they had hired more.[14]

Opinion: The firms that announce “AI layoffs” make the headlines. The far more common response is quieter: hiring a little less.

#### Japan: fewer layoffs, a different risk

Japan is in a different place. In the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications’ international comparison for fiscal 2024, 26.7% of individuals in Japan had used generative AI, against 68.8% in the US, 59.2% in Germany and 81.2% in China. One 2025 estimate puts the share of Japanese firms that have fully adopted generative AI in their core operations at just 1.9%, against 6.1% in the US, the lowest in the G7.[15]

The government’s line, for now, is that there is no major impact. In the House of Councillors on 8 July 2026, Takahiro Anno of the party Team Mirai cited the Stanford study and asked for regular monitoring. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare replied that, judging by youth unemployment, graduates’ job-finding rates and employment in IT, no major impact had arisen so far, including on young people.[17] A Japan Productivity Center survey published in September 2026 found more than 90% of firms saying AI had not yet changed their headcount, though more than half expect fewer staff in 5 to 10 years.[18]

The longer view is less calm. In the House of Representatives on 15 April 2026, Michio Kawai of the same party cited the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s March 2026 estimate of Japan’s job structure in 2040, which shows a surplus of office workers and a shortage of 3.39 million people able to work with AI and robots.[16]

Naoyuki Fukuda of the Japan Research Institute argues that Japan is unlikely to see a US-style rise in youth unemployment: labour shortages, long-term employment and the mass hiring of new graduates every spring act as a cushion. The risk is different. Japanese firms have trained new staff by giving them simple tasks first and letting them learn on the job. If generative AI takes over that starting point, a generation may “get a job, but never learn the work”, and the problem would surface only 5 to 10 years later, when that generation is meant to start managing.[15]

Opinion: In the US, the entrance is narrowing. In Japan, the entrance may stay open while the first rungs of the ladder disappear.

#### What a basic income could do in this kind of disruption

If AI were wiping out jobs across the board, the question would be how to replace the incomes of millions. The data so far show something narrower: fewer first jobs for young people in exposed fields, freelancers losing work task by task, and, in Japan, a possible loss of learning on the job. A basic income fits this particular shape in three ways.

First, a floor for people with no work history. Unemployment insurance, in Japan as elsewhere, pays only people who have worked and paid contributions. A graduate who never got a first job, or a freelancer whose clients drifted away, often gets nothing. The same is true of Japan’s new payment for workers (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/refundable-tax-credit-vs-basic-income/), which requires earned income in the previous year. A basic income reaches people whether or not they have worked before.

Second, time. Finding the next job, retraining or starting something new takes months. A small, steady income that does not stop when you go back to study or take a risky job makes those months possible.

Third, bargaining power. Someone with a floor can turn down a poor offer, or a contract at a fraction of the old rate, a little more easily. When work is bought task by task, that matters.

Cash trials give some evidence on whether people use the money this way. In Sam Altman’s OpenResearch study (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/), $1,000 a month for three years led recipients to work about 1.3 hours a week less than the control group, while employment rose in both groups. In Finland’s 2017–2018 experiment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/), 2,000 unemployed people received €560 a month; the employment effects were small, and wellbeing and trust improved. In Stockton, California (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-stockton), the share of recipients in full-time work rose from 28% to 40% in a year, more than twice the gain in the control group. None of these trials was about AI. They suggest that a modest floor does not make most people stop working, and that it gives them some room to choose.

Opinion: A basic income would not bring the jobs back. It would change what losing one, or never getting one, means.

#### The strongest case against

The most careful critique comes from a research brief published by the International Labour Organization in May 2026, “Why UBI is not the answer to the impact of AI on the labour market”, by Tuğba Özay and Ekkehard Ernst. It is a paper by named authors, not a formal ILO position. It argues that “AI transforms tasks, not occupations”, so mass unemployment is unlikely, and that a universal payment would push demand into sectors where supply is slow to grow, such as housing, health and care: “Distributing money faster than constrained supply can adjust produces inflation, not abundance.” It does concede that “cognitive jobs are seeing their skill premium eroding, especially for younger job market entrants”. It recommends retraining, active labour-market policy, portable benefits, more housing, taxing AI rents, and social protection that keeps work incentives, “for instance through an earned-income tax credit”.[19]

Robert Litan at the Brookings Institution proposes “transition insurance” instead. Anyone involuntarily displaced, with no need to prove that AI was the cause, and with at least three years in the job, would receive 80%, 60% and 40% of the earnings they lost in the first three years after finding new work. Adding lifetime training accounts and a tax credit for hiring recent graduates, he puts the cost at about $60 billion a year in all, against about $784 billion net for a poverty-level basic income, which he rejects as too expensive.[21]

These critiques deserve a fair hearing. The evidence above supports their first point: so far, AI has reshaped tasks and hiring far more than it has destroyed jobs. Litan’s plan is cheaper, and it would help the mid-career office worker whose pay falls after a layoff.

But both leave the same people out. Wage insurance pays only people who had a job and find another. An earned-income tax credit pays only people who already work. The graduate who never got a first job and the freelancer whose work never counted as employment fall through both, and they are exactly the people the data show being hit first. On inflation, the evidence from cash transfers is more mixed than the brief suggests. When GiveDirectly gave about $1,000 each to more than 10,500 poor households in rural Kenya, a shock worth over 15% of local GDP, researchers found large gains for neighbouring households and firms and “minimal price inflation”.[20] A one-off transfer in rural Kenya does not settle what would happen to rents in Tokyo, and the shortage of housing is a real problem whatever the policy. But more money does not automatically mean higher prices.

Opinion: Our reading: in the present situation, a basic income is not the only tool, and probably not the first one governments will reach for. It is the one that covers the people the other tools miss.

#### What is actually being tried

Small steps are already happening. The AI Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-ai-dividend), run by US nonprofits, began in March 2026 to pay $1,000 a month for a year, with no strings, to a group of 25 to 50 workers who lost work to AI. It is a demonstration rather than a study: there is no control group.

AI companies have started to publish proposals of their own. Anthropic’s economic policy framework of June 2026 sets out responses by the level of unemployment: at about 5%, training grants, wage insurance and incentives to keep and redeploy workers; at about 10%, expanded unemployment insurance as the priority; and at “unprecedented” levels, sustained income replacement, which “might include basic income, sovereign wealth models, and equity-sharing mechanisms”. Anthropic also pledged $200 million for research and policy trials.[22] Its Public Benefit Fund (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/public-benefit-fund/), which we have written about separately, is another commitment. OpenAI’s April 2026 paper “Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age” proposes a Public Wealth Fund that would give every American a stake in AI companies and infrastructure and pay the returns directly, along with safety nets that switch on automatically when displacement data cross a threshold. It does not name basic income.[23]

Lawmakers are moving too. H.R. 10044, introduced in the US House of Representatives in September 2026 by Sara Jacobs, Greg Casar and Valerie Foushee, would levy an excise tax on AI tokens or revenue that rises automatically with unemployment. The money would go to job creation, such as housing, infrastructure and care, not to cash payments.[24] In South Korea, President Lee Jae-myung said in an interview with The Economist in June 2026 that “a new mechanism such as basic income” is needed to share part of AI’s excess profits with ordinary people. His policy chief floated an “AI national dividend” paid from the windfall tax revenue of chipmakers, and the government then reframed it as using excess tax revenue in general. The newspaper Hankook Ilbo warned against going too fast and called funding the crux.[25]

How much would a floor cost? With the basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=jp&w=all&m=30000), ¥30,000 a month for everyone in Japan comes to about ¥44.2 trillion a year gross, about 6.7% of GDP. The net cost, after what comes back as tax, is much smaller, as our essay on refundable tax credits (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/refundable-tax-credit-vs-basic-income/) shows with a worked example.

Opinion: None of these is yet a basic income for the age of AI. But the question has moved, from “will AI take our jobs?” to “who pays for the transition, and how does the money reach people?”

#### Neither “AI is taking every job” nor “nothing is happening”

Opinion: Here is what the data show as of November 2026. AI is not yet visible in overall employment or unemployment, whether in the US, Denmark or Japan. Announced “AI layoffs” are real decisions by real companies, but they are a small and partly self-presented share of all cuts. At the same time, the entry door is narrowing for young people in exposed fields, freelancers have lost work, and Japan may be losing the first rungs on which people learn their trade.

Opinion: This is a disruption that falls first on the people with the least protection: those with no work history, no employer and no claim on unemployment insurance. That is where the simplest feature of a basic income, that it reaches everyone without asking whether you have worked, matters most. It is not the only answer, and its critics are right that it costs a great deal and that supply matters. But a floor that is ready before it is needed is easier to build than one improvised in a crisis.

Opinion: In part 2, we turn to creative work: illustrators, translators, writers and voice actors, where the change has come fastest.

### Refundable tax credits vs basic income: what Japan’s new payment for workers is, and is not

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/refundable-tax-credit-vs-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-06

On 6 November 2026, Japan’s House of Representatives passed a bill. It cuts the consumption tax on food to 1% for two years and creates the Worker Burden Relief Payment (shūgyōsha futan keigen shienkin), cash paid every year to low- and middle-income people who work, in proportion to their income. The government calls the payment the first step toward a “refundable tax credit”, an idea Japan has debated for years.[2][5]

Some people hear “refundable tax credit” and think of something close to basic income. Both link the tax system to cash payments. But the two differ sharply in who gets the money, on what conditions, and when. We first check what Japan has decided and what it has not, then set it beside examples from other countries and go through the differences one by one.

#### What Japan has decided, and what it has not

The flat ¥20,000 handout the ruling parties promised in the summer 2025 upper house election never happened, and the debate moved to a scheme that would pay every year according to income. On 18 December 2025 the Liberal Democratic Party and the Democratic Party for the People agreed to overhaul the personal allowances in income tax within three years, with a refundable tax credit or similar scheme in mind.[1]

The Social Security National Council, which began in February 2026, worked through cross-party working-level and expert meetings and issued an interim report on 29 July. It proposed introducing an “income-linked, finely tuned payment” in fiscal 2029, treating taxes, social insurance contributions and cash benefits together, with two aims: to raise the take-home pay of low- and middle-income workers, and to ease the “income walls” that lead people to hold back on work. Some members argued strongly that the ideal is a mix of tax credit and cash, but to avoid a complex system the council chose cash payments alone for now.[1]

On 15 September the cabinet approved an outline putting this into concrete form, and on 9 October it sent the bill to the Diet. From April 2027, for two years, the consumption tax on food falls from 8% to 1% (0.78% national plus local consumption tax). During those two years the payment starts early, capped at the revenue expected from one percentage point of the food tax. The full scheme begins in fiscal 2029, when the rate returns to 8%.[2][3]

The bill and the outline set out the rules. Eligibility is individual, and single people are included. A person qualifies if the previous year’s earned income (wages, plus business or freelance income above a set amount) is above a floor, total income is at or below a ceiling (the ceiling depends on the number of children), and the taxes and social insurance contributions they pay are above a set level. Pensioners who work and pay as much as working-age people are also covered. Once the full scheme starts, people whose spouse’s income is above a set amount are excluded.[2][3]

The amount is flat for people whose earned income is up to a level set with reference to the line below which no local income tax is due (¥1.19 million in wages for a single person). Above that it rises with earned income, levels off, and then, as total income rises further, falls to zero. There is a flat addition for each child aged 18 or under (under 16 in fiscal 2027 and 2028), and a temporary addition for people hitting an “income wall”, until those walls are removed.[2]

As a rule it is paid once a year. The municipality where the person lives confirms eligibility and pays within two months. For people who have registered a bank account for public payments, the municipality is meant to confirm eligibility on its own, with no application needed. The payment is not taxed and cannot be seized. The national government pays at least two thirds of the cost.[2][3]

What is not decided is the part that matters most: the amounts and the lines. The income floor, the ceiling and the payment amounts will all be set by cabinet order.[3] As “one reference”, the government told the parties in October that in fiscal 2027 and 2028 about 20 million people could be covered, with an average of about ¥30,000 a year each, about ¥600 billion a year in total, and that a ceiling somewhere in the ¥3 million range of individual annual income was possible.[4] For the floor, options of about ¥530,000, ¥740,000 and about ¥1.06 million in wages had been discussed in the council.[1]

The bill passed the lower house on 6 November with the votes of the Liberal Democratic Party, the Japan Innovation Party and others; every opposition party voted against. Upper house deliberations are expected to start the following week, but the ruling parties lack a majority there, so it is not yet clear whether the bill will become law before the session ends on 12 December.[5]

Opinion: So although it carries the name “refundable tax credit”, what Japan is building first is not a tax credit but an income-linked cash payment, aimed at low- and middle-income people who work. That is the starting point for comparing it with basic income.

#### What a refundable tax credit is

A tax credit is an amount subtracted from the tax you owe. But people who owe little tax cannot use all of it, so the lower your income, the less you gain. A refundable tax credit pays the part you could not use as cash.

One of its roots is the negative income tax, which the economist Milton Friedman popularised in Capitalism and Freedom in 1962. People whose income falls below a set line receive money from the government instead of paying tax. In the late 1960s and the 1970s the United States ran four large experiments to test the idea. In the largest, in Seattle and Denver (about 4,800 families), annual working hours fell by about 9% for husbands, about 20% for wives and about 14% for single mothers. An analysis that found more divorces caused controversy.[6] Mincome in Dauphin, Canada (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-mincome) was a guarantee of the same type, reduced by 50% of other income.

#### How other countries do it

The US Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is the best-known refundable tax credit. It grows with earnings, reaches a maximum, and then shrinks as income rises. For 2026, families with three or more children gain 45% of earnings up to $18,290, for a maximum of $8,231; people without children can get at most $664.[7] It is usually paid when the tax return is filed the following year.

Because you have to file to get it, some people miss out. The IRS estimates the national participation rate for tax year 2022 at 80.8% (78% in a separate estimate based on the Current Population Survey): about one in five people who could have claimed it did not.[8]

In 2021 the Child Tax Credit (CTC) was expanded for one year. It rose to $3,000 a year per child ($3,600 under age 6), was paid in full even to families with no income, and half of it was paid in advance every month from July to December. Child poverty on the Census Bureau’s Supplemental Poverty Measure fell to a record low of 5.2% in 2021, and after the expansion ended it more than doubled to 12.4% in 2022 (both as first published).[9] In 2025 it was 13.4%. Even so, refundable tax credits (the EITC and the refundable part of the CTC) lifted 3.3 million children above the poverty line in 2025.[10]

The UK took a different path. Working Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit have been replaced, along with other benefits, by Universal Credit. It is calculated every month from that month’s earnings. For people responsible for a child, or whose health limits their ability to work, the payment falls by 55p for every £1 earned above a monthly work allowance of £427 or £710. A couple is assessed as one household.[11]

The Canada Child Benefit uses tax returns to learn a family’s income and pays monthly. It does not ask whether anyone works. From July 2026 to June 2027 it pays up to C$8,157 a year for each child under 6 and C$6,883 for each child aged 6 to 17, reduced once the family’s previous-year net income exceeds C$38,237.[12]

#### Six differences from basic income

First, who gets it. A basic income goes to everyone. A refundable tax credit draws income lines and pays the people inside them. In Japan’s reference figures, about 20 million people would get the new payment.[4]

Second, whether work is a condition. The EITC and Japan’s payment are designed so that you get nothing without earned income and more once you start working, because they exist to encourage work. The flip side is that they do not reach people who cannot work because of illness, disability, caring or unemployment. Japan’s bill says the government will study measures for such people and reach a conclusion during fiscal 2028.[3] A basic income has no conditions at all.

Third, individual or household. The EITC is set by the tax unit (couples file jointly), Universal Credit by the household, and the Canada Child Benefit by family income. Japan’s payment is individual, which on this point is close to a basic income. Once the full scheme starts, however, people whose spouse earns above a set amount are excluded.[2]

Fourth, when it arrives. A basic income arrives every month, in advance. The EITC is paid after the year ends, through the tax return, and Japan’s payment is made once a year based on the previous year’s income. If your income falls sharply this year, it shows up only next year. The US paid the 2021 CTC in monthly instalments precisely to close this gap.

Fifth, missed payments. When a scheme needs a claim or a tax return, some people who qualify never get it. For the EITC it was about one in five.[8] Japan’s payment is designed to need no application for people with a registered account for public payments, but only about half of residents have registered one.[1]

Sixth, how it falls as income rises. Withdrawing a benefit as income rises works, for the person receiving it, just like a higher tax rate. Universal Credit’s 55% taper, combined with income tax and National Insurance, leaves even less of each extra pound. Every scheme phases out gradually to avoid a sudden “cliff”, but people inside the phase-out range carry a heavier effective burden. Japan’s extra amount for those facing an “income wall” is a response to this problem.[2][11]

#### The same, net

Having listed the differences, here is the twist: a negative income tax and a basic income can be designed to leave everyone with exactly the same final income. Simple numbers show how. The 30% used here is only for comparing the mechanics. It is not a funding estimate.

On the basic income side, everyone gets ¥360,000 a year (¥30,000 a month), and an extra 30% tax is added on all income. On the negative income tax side, a person with no income gets ¥360,000 a year, reduced by 30 sen for every yen of income. The payment reaches zero at an income of ¥1.2 million, and above that people pay 30% of the excess.

With no income, you receive ¥360,000 either way. With ¥1 million of income, under the basic income you receive ¥360,000 and pay ¥300,000, a net gain of ¥60,000; under the negative income tax, ¥360,000 minus ¥300,000 also leaves ¥60,000. With ¥3 million, under the basic income you receive ¥360,000 and pay ¥900,000, a net cost of ¥540,000; under the negative income tax you pay 30% of the ¥1.8 million above ¥1.2 million, again ¥540,000.

Opinion: The net result is identical. What differs is how the money flow looks, and the order in which it arrives. With a basic income, everyone receives the money first, and people with income hand some back as tax. That is why the gross amount paid out looks so large. With the basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=jp&w=all&m=30000), ¥30,000 a month for everyone in Japan comes to about ¥44.2 trillion a year gross, about 6.7% of GDP. In a 2017 paper the political philosopher Karl Widerquist calculated, for the United States, that the net cost, after subtracting what comes back as tax, is far smaller than the gross figure.[13]

Opinion: Put the other way round, the real difference between a basic income and a negative income tax is not the net amount. It is whether the money reaches everyone first, or reaches only people whose eligibility has been checked, and later. That difference decides how many people miss out, and whether the money helps right away when someone loses a job. When Heizo Takenaka explained his ¥70,000-a-month plan (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/takenaka-70000-yen-basic-income/), he too spoke of a negative tax rate for people on low incomes, and of paying everyone first and having high earners return it through their tax returns.

#### BIEN’s five criteria

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”.[14] We used this yardstick in our essay on Japan’s ¥100,000 payment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/). Here it is applied to the new Japanese payment.

Periodic? Yes, though only once a year.

Cash? Yes.

Individual? Mostly yes. Once the full scheme starts, people whose spouse’s income is above a set amount are excluded.

Universal? No. Only working people between the income floor and the ceiling.

Unconditional? No. It requires earned income and a certain level of taxes and social insurance contributions paid.[2][3]

Opinion: That is two and a half out of five. The US EITC, calculated per tax unit, conditional on work and limited by income, scores lower still. Missing criteria is less a design flaw than a sign of a different purpose. A refundable tax credit is a tool for lightening the load on people who work and making each extra hour pay. A basic income is a tool for giving everyone a floor, whether or not they work.

#### Three people, side by side

Finally, three examples. Japan’s amounts and lines are not yet set, so we use only the rules in the bill and the outline and the reference figures the government has given. The basic income is ¥30,000 a month (¥360,000 a year) for everyone.

A is looking for work and had no earned income last year. A gets no payment. A basic income would bring ¥360,000 a year, ¥30,000 each month.

B works part-time and earned ¥1 million in wages last year. Whether B qualifies depends on where the floor is set. With a floor of about ¥530,000 or ¥740,000 in wages, B qualifies and, being below the no-local-tax line, would likely receive the flat amount. With about ¥1.06 million, B does not qualify.[1][2] A basic income would bring ¥360,000 a year.

C is an office worker who earned ¥4.5 million in wages last year. That is above the ceiling in the government’s reference figures (individual income in the ¥3 million range), so C would likely get nothing.[4] A basic income would bring C ¥360,000 a year, but C would also pay more tax to fund it, so C could end up paying more, net.

Opinion: The new payment works best for someone like B, and does not reach A. A basic income gives all three the same amount and lets the tax system make the difference. Which is better depends on what you want to achieve.

#### A realistic first step?

Opinion: Refundable tax credits have strengths a basic income lacks. Because they target, the same budget goes further per person. Because take-home pay rises with work, they send a clear signal in favour of working. And agreement is easier to reach. In Japan, the parties in the national council did come together on introducing an income-linked payment in fiscal 2029. What divided them was the “bridge” tied to the consumption tax cut, and in the lower house vote every opposition party voted against.[1][5]

Opinion: What Japan’s payment is building, a way to know each person’s income and pay into their account without an application, is also the foundation any basic income would need. Remembering that the ¥100,000 of 2020 took months to reach some people because each bank account had to be checked by hand, that is no small thing.

Opinion: But its limits matter too. It does not reach people who cannot work, it arrives a year late, and only once a year. The reference amount of about ¥30,000 a year is one twelfth of a ¥30,000-a-month basic income. It is more accurate to see a refundable tax credit not as a substitute for basic income but as a tool that fills one gap in the current system. How far that tool grows will become clear as the amounts and lines are set ahead of the full launch in fiscal 2029. We will be watching.

### Did Finland’s basic income experiment fail? What it showed, and what it could not

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/
- Published: 2026-11-06

Bring up basic income and, sooner or later, someone will say it: “Finland already tried that, and it failed.”

This site supports basic income. That is exactly why we wanted to know whether “it failed” holds up, so we went back to the primary sources.

Opinion: The short answer: it was neither a failure nor a success. It was an experiment with a clear list of things it found, and an equally clear list of things it could not find out.

#### Where “failed” came from

It started in April 2018, when English-language media ran the story almost at once. Toru Yamamori of Doshisha University collected the headlines at the time: Business Insider (19 April) said Finland “is killing” its experiment, BBC News (23 April) that the trial “falls flat”, Sky News (24 April) that Finland would “scrap” it, the Orlando Sentinel (24 April) called it a “failed universal basic income experiment”, and USA Today (25 April) said it “didn’t work out”.[3]

Japanese media ran similar headlines in the same weeks, with words like “interrupted” and “terminated”.[1][2]

The idea stuck. In December 2019 Business Insider was still calling the trial “a major flop”, though the same headline went on: “But experts say the test was flawed.”[6]

Opinion: In April 2018, not a single result from the experiment had yet been published.

#### What the experiment actually was

The experiment was run by Kela, the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, for two years, from January 2017 to December 2018.[7][13]

2,000 people aged 25 to 58 were chosen at random from those receiving basic unemployment benefits from Kela in November 2016.[4][7]

Each received €560 a month, tax-free, for two years.

The €560 was not reduced if they found work or had other income, and they did not have to look for a job.

Taking part was compulsory. The unemployed people who were not chosen formed the control group.

According to Kela, it was the world’s first basic income experiment that was nationwide, set up by law and based on a randomised field experiment. The aim was to see whether removing the trap in which taking work cuts your benefits would help unemployed people into jobs.[7]

#### It was never “scrapped”

What was decided in April 2018 was not to stop the experiment. Kela had asked the government for extra money to widen it to people in work and to keep it going after 2018. The government said no.[2][4]

In other words, the experiment would end on schedule, after the two years originally planned. Kela quickly put out a release: “Contrary to reports, the Basic Income Experiment in Finland will continue until the end of 2018.”[5]

Yamamori wrote that neither decision had anything to do with the experiment failing to produce the hoped-for results, or with it having failed.[3] In any case, the analysis was set to begin only after the experiment ended: no findings were reported while it was running, so as not to influence how people in either group behaved.[7]

It is true, though, that the government of the day was not keen on basic income. From January 2018 it added an “activation model” to unemployment benefits: benefits were cut unless the person took part in training or worked at least 18 hours in three months.[3][4]

Kela’s Miska Simanainen told the Swedish newspaper Svenska Dagbladet, as quoted by the Guardian: “The government is making changes taking the system away from basic income.”[4]

#### Year-one results (February 2019)

The first results came out on 8 February 2019. In the first year, 2017, recipients were in work for an average of 49.64 days and the control group for 49.25 days: practically the same. No effect on employment was found.[8]

The survey told a different story. 55% of recipients rated their health as good or very good, against 46% of the control group. 17% of recipients reported feeling very stressed, against about a quarter of the control group.[8] Recipients also trusted other people more, scoring 6.8 out of 10 against 6.3.[10]

But only 31% of recipients and 20% of the control group answered the survey, so these figures need to be read with care.[9]

#### Final results (May 2020)

The final evaluation, covering both years, was published by the Ministry of Social Affairs and Health and Kela on 6 May 2020, under the title “small employment effects, better perceived economic security and mental wellbeing”.[11]

On work: over the year from November 2017 to October 2018, roughly the second year of the trial, recipients were in work about 6 days more than the control group, at 78 days on average.[11][12]

Six days in a year is not a big difference. Kari Hämäläinen of the VATT Institute for Economic Research summed it up: “All in all, the employment effects were small.”[13]

On wellbeing, the difference was clear. Compared with the control group, recipients were more satisfied with their lives and reported less mental strain, depression, sadness and loneliness, and a more positive view of their income and economic wellbeing. They trusted other people and the institutions of society more, and were more confident about their own future.[7]

#### What the experiment could not tell us

This is the most important part. The experiment had clear limits.

First, only unemployed people took part. People in work, students and pensioners were not included. It was not a test of a basic income paid to everyone.[4][7]

Second, it was short and small: two years and 2,000 recipients. Olli Kangas, an expert involved in the trial, told the broadcaster Yle that “two years is too short a period to be able to draw extensive conclusions from such a big experiment.”[4]

Third, it did not test the funding side. For a basic income paid to everyone, the biggest question is how to raise the money through taxes. The experiment did not change the tax system.

Fourth, the activation model arrived in the second year. The new rules did not affect the two groups in the same way, so it is impossible to say how much of the second-year difference was due to basic income.[7][13]

Kela itself writes that basic income increased activity and employment among people who were already active before the experiment, but did not solve the problems of those who were in a difficult situation.[7]

Opinion: Put together, this is what the experiment showed: giving unemployed people money with no conditions for two years did not make them stop working. Nor did it make them work much more. But it did make them feel more secure and better in themselves.

Opinion: The experiment does not answer the question “can basic income work as a national system?” And a question it did not answer cannot be called either a failure or a success.

#### Compared with other experiments

In Stockton (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-stockton), California (2019–2021), 125 residents received $500 a month for two years. In the first year, the share of recipients in full-time work rose from 28% to 40%, more than the rise of about 5 points in the control group.[14][15]

In OpenResearch’s study (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/) (2020–2023), 1,000 people aged 21 to 40 received $1,000 a month for three years. They worked about 1.3 hours a week less, but the share in work rose in both groups (from 58% to 72% among recipients and from 59% to 74% in the control group).

GiveDirectly’s study in Kenya (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-kenya) (2017–) is a large experiment that includes a group paid for 12 years. Early results found that the total amount of work did not change, but people shifted from wage work towards self-employment.[16]

Opinion: None of these experiments found that “give people money and they stop working”. None found a magic way to make people work much more, either. Finland’s results fit this pattern well.

The key facts about the Finnish experiment are also on its card in our timeline (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-finland).

#### Finland since

In 2026 Finland is moving in the opposite direction from basic income. On 1 May 2026, Kela’s two unemployment benefits, the labour market subsidy and the basic unemployment allowance, were merged into a new “general support” (yleistuki). Kela notes that, unlike the basic allowance, the general support is means-tested: capital income and other income can reduce it.[17]

The debate goes on. In March 2026 the Finnish Parliament’s information service costed four basic income models built on €260 a month, and the Greens published the memo.[18] In the city of Lahti, councillors proposed a local basic income trial. In June 2026 a city committee turned it down, saying the city has no power to run one, but its reply still described the 2017–2018 experiment as having had positive effects on wellbeing while its employment effects stayed small.[19]

#### What to take from it

The April 2018 “scrapped” and “failed” headlines were wrong. The experiment ran its full two years as planned; the government only declined to extend and widen it. And no results had been published yet.

In the final results, the effect on work was small (about 6 days), while life satisfaction, mental wellbeing and trust improved.

Only unemployed people took part, it lasted two years, and the funding side was never tested. In the second year, another policy change got in the way.

Opinion: So you cannot say “basic income failed”, and you cannot say “basic income succeeded”. What you can say is: the money did not make people stop working, it did not make them work much more, and it made their lives feel more secure.

Opinion: Next time someone tells you “Finland already tried it and it failed”, try asking: what exactly failed? The answer is more interesting than they think.

### ¥70,000 a month for everyone: who gains and who loses? Heizo Takenaka’s basic income plan, worked out for five households

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/takenaka-70000-yen-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-06

“¥70,000 a month for everyone.” In 2020 the economist Heizo Takenaka put this idea on Japanese television and set off a storm. Takenaka served as minister for economic and fiscal policy and as minister for internal affairs in Junichiro Koizumi’s government (2001–2006), and was then chairman of the staffing company Pasona Group.[1] “Nobody can live on ¥70,000.” “So you want to scrap pensions?” Posts citing his plan still turn up on Japanese social media today.

This site supports basic income, but not any particular plan. So before deciding for or against, we start with a more down-to-earth question: if this plan came true, would your household end up with more money or less?

Opinion: The short answer is: it depends on the design. The same ¥70,000 can be a gain or a loss, depending on what it replaces and who has to pay it back later. Below we put numbers on that range.

#### What Takenaka proposed

It started on the evening of 23 September 2020, on the BS-TBS news programme Hōdō 1930. The programme presented Takenaka’s view on a panel that read “¥70,000 a month to every citizen.”[1]

According to reports, incomes would be tracked by linking people’s My Number identification numbers to their bank accounts, and anyone above a certain income would pay the money back after receiving it. Asked on the programme whether pensions and public assistance would then become unnecessary, Takenaka reportedly answered, “Basically, yes.”[2]

Some background for readers outside Japan. Japan’s public pension (nenkin) has two layers: a flat-rate basic pension that everyone can earn, called the National Pension, and, for people who worked as employees, an earnings-related top-up called the Employees’ Pension. Public assistance (seikatsu hogo) is the means-tested safety net of last resort: it pays living costs, rent and medical care for people who have no other way to get by.

His book, published in August 2020, put it bluntly: “The plan to pay each person ¥70,000 a month is also a trade-off for abolishing social security such as pensions and public assistance. If we pay ¥70,000 to every citizen, we can get rid of pensions for the elderly and the cost of public assistance.”[3][4]

#### The backlash, and his explanation

Criticism came fast. “Nobody can live on ¥70,000 a month each.” “Isn’t this just a cut to social security?” J-CAST News reported that comments like these flooded the internet.[1] Genki Sudo, then a member of the House of Councillors, posted, “Are you telling pensioners to starve to death?” and wrote that a basic income would need to be at least ¥200,000 a month.[2]

On 7 October 2020, Takenaka sat down with J-CAST News. In summary, he said:[1]

He had never said anyone could live on ¥70,000. ¥70,000 was an average, and at that level the cost to public finances would not be too heavy.

A family of four might not need ¥280,000, so the third and fourth members could get less, and in exchange a person living alone could get a little more.

Pensions would switch to basic income while protecting what people had already paid in. Public assistance could also remain, as a top-up.

It would work like progressive taxation: high earners pay a high rate, and people on low incomes pay a negative rate, meaning they receive money.

Paying everyone first and having high earners return it later through their tax returns was not a bad method, because no one can tell in advance who will need help.

Opinion: “A trade-off for abolishing” pensions and public assistance, in the book, and “protecting what people paid in” with public assistance “as a top-up”, in the interview, leave very different impressions. Which one is the real plan? No detailed design has been published. And it is exactly this unclear part that matters most once you do the household sums.

#### Where ¥70,000 came from

According to J-CAST News, Takenaka’s plan builds on the views of the economist Yutaka Harada. In his 2015 book Basic Income: Can the State Solve Poverty? and elsewhere, Harada proposed ¥70,000 a month for everyone aged 20 and over and ¥30,000 a month for those under 20. Takenaka seems to have broadened this to “around ¥70,000” with a progressive structure, the article says.[1][5]

¥70,000 is also close to the full basic pension. In fiscal 2026 the full National Pension is ¥70,608 a month.[6]

Among political parties, the Japan Innovation Party (Nippon Ishin no Kai) said at its April 2021 convention that it would put a basic income, framed as a guaranteed minimum income, in its platform. Then too, a big point of debate was that paying everyone would need around ¥100 trillion a year.[7]

#### Our assumptions

Since Takenaka has not set out a detailed design, we fix our assumptions first.

The amount is ¥70,000 a month per person, children included, as on the programme’s panel. For the four-person households we also show the case where children get Harada’s ¥30,000.

Pensions are calculated three ways. (A) Pensions stay as they are and basic income is added on top. (B) Only the basic pension is replaced by basic income, and the earnings-related Employees’ Pension top-up is protected. (C) Pensions are replaced by basic income entirely.

Public assistance is calculated two ways. (A) Public assistance covers whatever basic income does not. (B) Public assistance is abolished.

The child allowance (jidō teate) is replaced by basic income, as in most basic income plans.

For the clawback from high earners, no income threshold or amount has been given, so we show both ends: nothing paid back, and everything paid back.

Tax rises or contribution changes to fund the plan are left out, because none have been specified. Any tax rise would lower every household’s result by that much.

All amounts are monthly, under the rules for fiscal 2026.

The current figures come from official sources. Pensions: the full National Pension is ¥70,608 a month, and the government’s model couple, a husband who worked 40 years on average pay and a wife who stayed at home, receives ¥237,279 a month, including two basic pensions.[6] Public assistance: a single person aged 20 to 40 in Tokyo’s 23 wards (the highest cost-of-living grade, 1-1) gets ¥77,220 a month for living costs (¥46,930 + ¥27,790 + a ¥2,500 special addition), and housing assistance for rent of up to ¥53,700 for a single person in Tokyo. That makes up to ¥130,920 a month, and medical care is covered separately, with nothing to pay.[8][9] Child allowance: ¥10,000 a month for each first or second child from age 3 up to high-school age, with no income limit since October 2024.[10]

#### Five households, worked out

1. A single office worker in their twenties, living alone in Tokyo, earning ¥3 million a year. They receive no benefits now, so the full ¥70,000 is added. In Takenaka’s explanation, it is “people with high incomes” who pay it back, and ¥3 million a year is unlikely to count. So they receive ¥70,000 a month, ¥840,000 a year. Any tax rise to fund the scheme would come out of that. Their answer: up to ¥70,000 a month, less whatever tax rises take.

2. A couple with two primary-school children, earning ¥5 million a year. They now get ¥20,000 a month in child allowance for the two children. With a flat basic income, the family gets ¥280,000 a month: even after losing the child allowance, that is ¥260,000 a month more. If children get less, as Takenaka suggested, and we use Harada’s ¥30,000, basic income comes to ¥200,000 and the net gain is ¥180,000 a month. Families with children are the most likely winners under this plan. Again, these figures are before any tax rise.

3. A retired couple: a husband who worked for a company and a wife who stayed at home. Their pensions now total ¥237,279 a month: ¥141,216 in two basic pensions and ¥96,063 in the husband’s Employees’ Pension top-up.[6] Basic income for two is ¥140,000. The result depends heavily on what happens to pensions. (A) Added on top: ¥377,279 a month, ¥140,000 more. (B) Only the basic pension replaced: ¥140,000 + ¥96,063 = ¥236,063, just ¥1,216 a month less, almost unchanged. (C) Pensions replaced entirely: ¥140,000 only, ¥97,279 a month less.

Case (C) is what Sudo was worried about. What Takenaka described in the interview, protecting what people paid in, is close to (B). A couple who only have the National Pension, such as former self-employed people (¥141,216 for two at the full rate), end up with about the same in every case. People who could not pay contributions for some years and do not get the full pension would gain.

4. A single person in their thirties on public assistance in Tokyo’s 23 wards. They now receive up to ¥130,920 a month for living costs and rent.[8] (A) If public assistance tops up basic income: ¥70,000 plus ¥60,920 in assistance, the same total as now. (B) If public assistance is abolished: ¥70,000 only, ¥60,920 a month less. Help with rent would disappear, and they might have to start paying for medical care.

The book’s “get rid of the cost of public assistance” is (B); the interview’s “public assistance can remain as a top-up” is (A). For this household, which one it is decides everything.

5. A couple with two children, earning ¥10 million a year. They now get ¥20,000 a month in child allowance. Basic income for four is ¥280,000 a month, and this is where “high earners pay it back later” comes in. If they keep it: ¥260,000 a month more, even after losing the child allowance. If they pay it all back: none of the basic income stays with them, and they are ¥20,000 a month worse off by the lost child allowance. A ¥10 million household is likely to be on the paying-back side, and any tax rise to fund the plan would fall heavily on this group. Realistically, expect somewhere between roughly zero and a loss.

In summary (monthly, before any tax rise):

| Household | Benefits now | Basic income | Net change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Single, 20s, ¥3m a year | None | ¥70,000 | +¥70,000 (less any tax rise) |
| Family of four, ¥5m a year | Child allowance ¥20,000 | ¥200,000–¥280,000 | +¥180,000 to +¥260,000 |
| Retired couple (former employee) | Pensions ¥237,279 | ¥140,000 | +¥140,000 to −¥97,279 (depends on pensions) |
| Single, on public assistance (Tokyo 23 wards) | Up to ¥130,920 | ¥70,000 | ±0 to −¥60,920 (depends on whether assistance stays) |
| Family of four, ¥10m a year | Child allowance ¥20,000 | ¥280,000 | +¥260,000 to −¥20,000 (depends on clawback) |

The likely winners are households with children and few benefits today. Those who could lose are people who rely on pensions or public assistance, and high-earning households that would pay the money back or bear the tax rises.

Opinion: The complaint that “nobody can live on ¥70,000” mostly concerns the cases where pensions or public assistance disappear. Takenaka’s reply that he “never said you could live on it” reads as assuming that some other benefits remain. Line up the assumptions, and both claims can be checked with numbers.

#### What would it cost the country?

After the household purse, the national one. Japan’s population is 122,812,000 (Statistics Bureau, final estimate as of 1 May 2026).[11] Paying everyone ¥70,000 a month for a year comes to ¥70,000 × 12 × 122,812,000, about ¥103.2 trillion.

Japan’s general account budget for fiscal 2026 is ¥122.3092 trillion, of which social security spending is ¥39.0559 trillion.[12] The basic income would be about 84% of the entire general account, and about 2.6 times social security spending.

Takenaka says the money for pensions and public assistance would be redirected.[3] Social security benefits as a whole, pensions and medical care included and counting contributions, come to ¥144.1 trillion. Of that, pensions are ¥63.7 trillion.[13] Even if every pension went into basic income, it would still be about ¥40 trillion short of ¥103 trillion.

The gap can be closed only by shrinking the real cost through the clawback from high earners, or by raising taxes. Where the clawback line is drawn changes both the funding needed and the results in the table above. You can try other amounts and groups in our basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=jp&w=all&m=70000): ¥70,000 a month for everyone is about 15.5% of GDP.

#### What to take from it

Takenaka’s plan, as shown on television in September 2020, was ¥70,000 a month for everyone, with high earners paying it back later. His book framed it as a trade-off for abolishing pensions and public assistance.

He later said ¥70,000 was an average, that he had never said anyone could live on it, that pensions already paid for would be protected and that public assistance could stay. On the point that matters most, his book and his interview disagree.

What it means for households depends on the design. Families with children are likely to gain a lot. For people who rely on pensions or public assistance, the result ranges from “about the same” to “tens of thousands of yen, up to nearly ¥100,000, less each month”, depending on whether those benefits survive.

Paying everyone would cost about ¥103 trillion a year. Even all of the pension money would not cover it, so the clawback and tax design cannot be skipped.

Opinion: When judging a basic income plan, it is worth looking past the amount to two questions: what is it traded for, and who pays it back? The same “¥70,000 a month” can be an entirely different system depending on the answers.

In 2020 Japan did pay ¥100,000 to everyone, once, as the Special Cash Payment. We looked at how that money was used, with data, in our essay on the ¥100,000 payment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/).

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/refundable-tax-credit-vs-basic-income/
