### What happened when Sam Altman’s study gave people $1,000 a month for three years

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/
- Published: 2026-11-04

In July 2024, the results came out of the largest study of no-strings cash in the United States, the one Sam Altman had backed. Within days the same numbers carried opposite headlines. One camp read “free money makes people work less”. The other read “cash gives people freedom”. Both were quoting the same papers.

This essay goes back to those papers: what the study was, what recipients did with the money and the time, what did not change, and what it does and does not tell us about basic income. It also asks why an AI company’s chief executive wanted to know.

#### What the study was

OpenResearch, a lab that began as Y Combinator Research, enrolled 3,000 people aged 21 to 40 whose household income in 2019 was no more than 300% of the federal poverty level, in 19 counties of northern Illinois (including the Chicago area) and north central Texas (including the Dallas area), in cities, suburbs and rural places.[1][2] Enrolment ran from October 2019 to October 2020. People were then randomly split: 1,000 received $1,000 a month and 2,000 received $50 a month as the control group, from November 2020 to October 2023. Two local non-profits made the payments.[2]

The money was fully unconditional. Nothing was required about work or spending, and payments continued whether or not someone kept answering the surveys.[1][2] Participants’ household income averaged about $29,900 in 2019, so $1,000 a month was roughly a 40% raise for the household.[2] The analysis was pre-registered, and the surveys reached 96% of participants at the end.[2]

By our arithmetic the transfers alone come to about $39.6 million: $36 million for the 1,000 recipients and $3.6 million for the control group. Forbes reported that OpenResearch and its entities had raised some $60 million since 2015, including $14 million donated by Altman, $10 million from OpenAI’s non-profit arm, $15 million from Jack Dorsey’s Start Small and $6.5 million from the GitLab co-founder Sid Sijbrandij.[3] The research itself also acknowledges a National Science Foundation grant.[2]

The reason goes back to January 2016, when Altman announced the study on Y Combinator’s blog. He wrote that “as technology continues to eliminate traditional jobs and massive new wealth gets created”, some version of basic income was likely to appear at a national scale, and that there was “fairly little data about how it would work”. He also asked: “Do people sit around and play video games, or do they create new things?”[4]

#### The headline: a little less work

The employment paper, by Eva Vivalt, Elizabeth Rhodes, Alexander Bartik, David Broockman, Patrick Krause and Sarah Miller, finds that recipients worked about 1.3 hours a week less than the control group in the surveys, and 1.4 to 1.5 hours less in the phone-app time diaries and time-use surveys. In the surveys they were 2.3 percentage points less likely to be employed. Their own income, not counting the transfers, was about $1,900 a year lower. Their partners cut their hours by a similar amount: together, participant and partner worked 2.1 hours a week less.[2]

Put another way, for every dollar received, household income from other sources fell by about 28 cents, and the participant’s own income by about 16 cents. The authors call the effect on hours and income a 5 to 6% decline relative to the control group, “a moderate effect”.[2]

Two details matter for the headline. First, employment rose in both groups over the three years, from 58% to 72% among recipients and from 59% to 74% in the control group; the controls simply rose further.[5] Counting the transfers, recipients’ own income in the third year was still about $10,000 higher than the control group’s.[5] Second, the numbers have moved. The first version of the paper (July 2024) put the fall in income at about $1,500 a year and the drop in labour market participation at 2.0 percentage points. The revision of August 2026, whose preferred measures combine survey answers with state unemployment-insurance records, puts them at about $1,900 and 4.2 percentage points.[2]

Opinion: Credit where it is due: the researchers revised their own headline effect upward, in the direction that is less convenient for the cause the study is associated with, and put the larger numbers in the abstract. That is what a study is for.

#### What they did with the time

According to the paper, the hours freed from work went mostly to leisure, along with some extra time driving and on other activities. The authors can rule out even small changes in time spent on childcare, exercise, job search or self-improvement.[2] The OpenResearch summary breaks the leisure down further: the largest increases were in driving, social leisure (time with other people: socialising, recreation, meals) and errands such as grocery shopping.[5]

Job search changed shape rather than stopping. Spells without work were about 0.8 months longer than the control group’s average of 7.8 months, and recipients were more likely to have recently applied for a job but applied to fewer positions.[2] Among those looking for work, recipients were 5.5 percentage points more likely to say that interesting or meaningful work was essential for any job they would take.[5] Even so, across a long list of measures, job quality did not improve, and the paper can rule out even small improvements in it, or wage gains above 58 cents an hour.[2]

Averages hide very different lives. One recipient, Nathan, cut his 50-hour week in half to spend time with his four-year-old son. Lisa took a lower-paid job with room to grow, used the transfers to cover the gap, and two years later was on a salary close to six figures. Shawn, who had been working 72 hours a week, decided to take a break before he burned out.[5] The patterns by group are exploratory, but the drop in work was concentrated among people under 30, single parents and those with the highest household incomes at the start; for recipients over 30 there was no significant effect on employment or hours.[5] Younger participants also showed larger estimated effects on further education, although there was no significant effect on degrees overall.[2]

#### What they did with the money

On average, recipients spent $310 a month more than the control group, and more than half of that went to basics: food ($67), rent ($52) and transport ($50). The biggest increase relative to what the control group spent was in financial support to others, such as gifts and loans to family and friends: $22 a month, 26% more.[6] People who started out below or near the poverty line drove the increase in spending; for the highest-income group the effect on total spending was small and not significant.[6]

The consumption paper estimates that spending rose by at least $300 a month, mostly on housing, food and cars, and that recipients were more likely to move to a new home and a new neighbourhood. Self-reported financial health and credit scores improved. But small gains in assets were offset by more debt, leaving net worth almost unchanged, and there was no effect on delinquencies, bankruptcies or foreclosures. The authors conclude that large temporary transfers “may not cause persistent improvements in the financial position of young, low-income households”.[7]

#### Health, children and attitudes to work

Health: the transfers brought large but short-lived improvements in stress and food security, and more use of hospital, emergency and dental care. They did not improve self-reported physical health, blood-test measures or mental health after the first year, and there was no effect on the health of children in the household.[8] OpenResearch notes that the first year overlapped with pandemic relief and that rising prices and the end of that aid may have worn the early gains down, but it says it cannot be sure why they faded.[8]

Children: a 2025 paper finds that parents who received $1,000 a month spent more on their children and reported closer supervision. They also reported more developmental difficulties and stress in their children, which the authors suggest may come from watching them more closely. Most outcomes in school records did not change meaningfully.[9]

Politics and work: a paper from December 2024 finds no effect on voting or political engagement and few changes in political views. One result runs against the stereotype: recipients came to see work as slightly more important for individuals and for society, and were more likely to support work requirements for Medicaid.[10] On Altman’s other question, creating new things, recipients were more likely to have a business idea and to say they intended to start one, but on average they were not significantly more likely to start a business. In an exploratory breakdown, Black and female recipients were more likely to have started or helped start one by the third year.[11]

#### The same results, two headlines

Coverage at the time was mostly careful. NPR reported that recipients worked “an hour or so less a week on average” and spent mostly on basics, and that the report itself says its results “provide support for both sides”. Chris Hughes, a co-founder of the Economic Security Project, which campaigns for guaranteed income, said: “I hope that people are taking away from this study and other studies that a guaranteed income will not work alone.” Michael Strain of the American Enterprise Institute preferred bigger tax credits for low-income workers, paid only to those who take a job.[12]

CBS quoted Vivalt: “From an economist’s point of view, it’s a moderate effect.” She did not see the lost hours as a failure: “People are doing more stuff, and if the results say people value having more leisure time — that this is what increases their well-being — that’s positive.” But on the hope that a cushion would lead to better jobs, she said: “we don’t find any effects on the quality of employment whatsoever.”[13] The same CBS article also said that 3,000 participants received $1,000 a month; in fact 1,000 did, and the other 2,000 got $50. It is a common slip, and it makes the study sound three times bigger than it was.[13][2] Writing in Fortune that September, Jesús Gerena, chief executive of the non-profit UpTogether, argued that the conclusions reporters and researchers drew were “rooted in painful stereotypes about people experiencing poverty, such as depicting them as lazy”.[14]

Opinion: Both short versions lose something. “Free money makes people lazy” does not fit a drop of about 5% in hours, in a period when employment rose in both groups, among people who came to value work a little more. “Cash transforms lives” does not fit a study that found no better jobs, no lasting gains in health or well-being, and net worth that barely moved. What the evidence shows is smaller and more useful: people treated the money as income, spent most of it on basics, and some of them used it to buy back time. Whether that time is “waste” or “freedom” is a value judgement the data cannot make for you.

#### Is this basic income?

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”, and lists five characteristics: periodic, cash, individual, universal and unconditional.[15]

Periodic? Yes, every month. Cash? Yes. Individual? Yes, it was paid to the person, not the household. Unconditional? Yes, with no work or spending rules. Universal? No. It went to 1,000 randomly chosen lower-income adults aged 21 to 40, for three years.

Opinion: So this was a guaranteed income trial, not a basic income, and three limits follow. First, it was temporary, and everyone knew when it would end; people might act differently, in either direction, if the payment were for life. Second, only a few people in each place received it, so it cannot show what a payment to everyone would do to rents, prices or wages, or what the taxes to fund it would change. Altman’s own post said that questions about the overall cost of living were “beyond our scope, but obviously important”.[4] Third, it ran through the pandemic and its aftermath, although the paper notes that its estimates mostly reflect 2022 and 2023.[2] What a randomised trial can show well is how individuals respond to extra income, and that is exactly the number any design for a larger scheme needs.

Finland’s 2017–2018 experiment, which paid €560 a month to 2,000 unemployed people for two years, had similar limits and a similar pattern: little change in work, a clear gain in wellbeing. We look at what it did and did not show (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/) in a separate essay.

OpenResearch says it kept surveying participants after the payments ended, through 2025.[1] We have not yet found published results from that period. It has also made the survey data available to researchers under a data use agreement, and the code for the employment paper is open; both are on our open data list (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/open-source/#data-openresearch-ucs).

#### Why it matters for AI

Altman’s 2016 question came from a worry about technology and jobs.[4] In 2021, in “Moore’s Law for Everything”, he went further and proposed an American Equity Fund, filled by taxing large companies and land, that would pay every adult a yearly share.[16] Our essay on universal high income (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/) looked at that plan and asked who pays. Since then, the money has started to appear on a small scale: the AI Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-ai-dividend) pays $1,000 a month for a year to workers hurt by AI, and Anthropic has set aside shares in a fund that could make direct distributions to specific populations (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/public-benefit-fund/).

Opinion: For anyone designing an AI-funded payment, this study gives planning numbers rather than a verdict. Most of the money goes on rent, food and transport. Recipients and their partners work a little less, so the cost has to count about 28 cents of other household income lost for each dollar paid. Short-term relief is large and real; lasting change in health, jobs or wealth is not something three years of $1,000 delivered on its own. A permanent dividend paid to everyone is a different policy and may behave differently, but this is the best evidence we have about how people respond.

#### What to take from it

Opinion: Altman asked an honest question in 2016 and paid for a careful answer, and the answer did not simply flatter the idea. The researchers published the null results alongside the good ones, revised their main estimate upward, and opened their data. That is worth more than any single headline.

Opinion: If you share one line from this study, make it the accurate one: 1,000 lower-income people received $1,000 a month for three years; they worked about 1.3 hours a week less, spent mostly on basics, felt better for a year, and many used the money to choose how they spent their time. Read it the way this site reads every free lunch: who paid, who received, and for how long.

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/public-benefit-fund/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/moltbook-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/finland-basic-income-experiment/

3. Forbes (via Forbes Australia) — OpenAI founder Sam Altman gave thousands of people free money. Here’s what happened (Sarah Emerson, 22 Jul 2024): https://www.forbes.com.au/news/innovation/openai-founder-sam-altman-gave-thousands-of-people-free-money/

### Where did the ¥100,000 go? Japan’s 2020 Special Cash Payment, by the data

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/
- Published: 2026-11-04

Between the spring and summer of 2020, almost everyone living in Japan received ¥100,000. It was called the Special Cash Payment (tokubetsu teigaku kyūfukin), and about ¥12.67 trillion was paid out in all. So what did people do with it? Some say it mostly ended up in savings accounts; others say it kept households afloat.

This question can, to a fair degree, be answered with data. We read the studies that used bank-account and budgeting-app records, along with the government’s own analysis, to see how much was spent, when, and by which households. Then we separate what this experience tells us about basic income from what it does not.

#### How the ¥100,000 was paid

Everyone recorded in the Basic Resident Register on 27 April 2020 was eligible, foreign residents included, for ¥100,000 each. The person entitled to receive it was the head of the household the person belonged to. Heads of household either mailed back the form their municipality had sent them with their bank details, or applied online through Mynaportal, and the money was in principle paid into an account in the applicant’s own name. The programme was budgeted at ¥12,880.293 billion (¥12,734.414 billion in payments and ¥145.879 billion in administration), all of it paid by the national government.[1]

The first plan was different. The government initially proposed ¥300,000 per household for households whose income had fallen sharply because of COVID-19; on 16 April 2020 it switched to ¥100,000 for every person.[2]

Payments began in May. By 26 June about ¥9.12 trillion (71.6%) had been paid, and by 31 July about ¥12.32 trillion. The final total was about ¥12.67 trillion, 99.7% of the amount municipalities had planned to pay: nearly everyone eligible was reached.[3]

When it arrived, though, depended a lot on where you lived. In Japan, bank accounts are not linked to resident records, so municipalities had to collect and check account numbers one by one.[2] Even within Tokyo, 85% of applicants in Nerima ward had been paid by 30 June, against 34.5% in Edogawa ward.[4]

Those delays turned out to be a gift to researchers. If, in the same week, some households have already been paid and others have not, comparing them separates the effect of the payment itself from the spread of the virus and the stay-at-home requests. All the studies below use this “natural experiment.”[2][4]

#### How much was spent?

So Kubota, Koichiro Onishi and Yuta Toyama of Waseda University studied about 2.8 million accounts at Mizuho Bank. Spending jumped in the week the money arrived and stayed moderately higher for more than a month. Within six weeks, outflows from the accounts equalled 49% of the payment; counting only cash withdrawals, 31%. Because those outflows include transfers and direct debits, the authors present this as an upper bound on spending.[4]

Michiru Kaneda, So Kubota and Satoshi Tanaka used data from 232,589 users of the budgeting app Money Forward ME. Within six weeks, 16% of the payment was spent under their baseline definition: 6% counted narrowly and 27% counted broadly.[2][5]

Takahiro Hattori and colleagues used the city-level figures of the government’s Family Income and Expenditure Survey and estimated that about 10% was spent in the month the payment arrived. Spending on things bought at home and in shops rose; spending on face-to-face services did not.[6]

In 2023 the Cabinet Office looked at data from another budgeting app, Moneytree, over 16 weeks from five weeks before to ten weeks after payment, and estimated that about 22% of the payment was spent. A check with the household survey’s individual records gave about 17% over roughly 16 weeks, broadly the same.[7]

Opinion: The numbers range from 6% to 49%. They depend on what counts as spending (whether withdrawn cash is assumed to be spent, whether transfers are included) and on how many weeks are measured. But they point the same way. In the weeks and months after the money arrived, studies that count spending narrowly found between a tenth and just under 30% spent, and even those that count every outflow found about half. The rest, at least, was not spent straight away.

This may not be a pandemic-only number. According to the Cabinet Office report, the 1999 regional promotion vouchers raised spending by about 32% of the amount given, and the 2009 fixed-sum benefit by about 33% in a survey, or about 25% from the month before receipt to two months after in an analysis of the household survey.[7] Hattori and colleagues also write that their roughly 10% is no different from estimates made before the pandemic.[6]

#### Who spent it?

The clearest finding, in every study, is that households with little money at hand spent more of the payment. In the Money Forward data, households whose liquid assets were smaller than their monthly earnings (19% of users) responded strongly, especially in the week of payment.[2] In the Mizuho data, households short of liquid funds spent nearly 60% of the payment. What mattered was not total financial assets but the balance in ordinary deposit accounts: “wealthy hand-to-mouth” households, with shares or insurance but little in their ordinary accounts, also spent a lot.[4]

On income, the studies disagree. The Cabinet Office found that households in the bottom third by equivalised income (income adjusted for household size) spent about 32% of the payment, with no clear effect for the middle and top thirds.[7] The Money Forward data also show a larger response in the quarter of households with the lowest earnings.[2] The Mizuho data, by contrast, show almost no difference by income; the difference there was for households whose income had fallen by more than half from the year before (54%).[4]

On age and household type, the Money Forward data give some clues. The older the household head, the bigger the response; people living alone responded less than other households, and married households more than single ones. Having children made little difference.[2] But budgeting-app users skew young and towards Tokyo, and include few women (partly, the authors suggest, because the payment went to household heads), so older households are hard to see in these data.[2][7]

#### Where did the unspent money go?

Some surveys simply asked people. In June 2020 the NLI Research Institute asked 2,062 people aged 20 to 69 what they used it for (more than one answer allowed). “Covering living costs” came first at 53.7%, followed by “savings” at 26.1%, “domestic travel” at 10.1%, “buying home appliances” and “buying masks and other hygiene products” at 9.7% each, “eating out” at 9.0% and “children’s education” at 7.0%. Only 9.7% said they saved all of it. The survey did not ask about amounts, however, and the researcher, Naoko Kuga, notes that measured in yen, more may have stayed in savings.[8]

Why keep it? In the same survey, people who chose savings were more likely than average to worry about losing income or their job. Kuga reads this as saving on purpose out of anxiety rather than having nothing to spend on during the stay-at-home period.[9] The Cabinet Office likewise says the part not spent right away probably built up as “excess savings,” helped by the restrictions on going out, and is expected to be drawn down later to support spending.[7]

Opinion: It is too early to say the money was wasted because it was saved. Covering living costs is itself spending. And ¥100,000 kept aside when no one could see what was coming was a kind of safety net for a household. Lifting the economy and supporting people’s lives have to be measured with different yardsticks. The Cabinet Office report itself says the programme did not necessarily have stimulating consumption as its direct aim.[7]

#### One-off ¥100,000 and basic income

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement,” and lists five characteristics: periodic, cash, individual, universal and unconditional.[10] It is the same yardstick we used in the essay on Thailand’s 10,000 baht (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/). Let’s run the ¥100,000 through it one by one.

Universal? Nearly, yes. Everyone on the resident register was eligible, foreign residents included.

Unconditional? Yes. There was no means test and no work requirement.

Cash? Yes. It could be spent on anything.

Periodic? No. It was paid once.

Individual? Strictly speaking, no. The household head applied for the whole family, and the money went into the household head’s account.[1][4] People who had fled domestic violence could, if they came forward, receive their own share and that of family members with them from the municipality they had fled to rather than the one where they were registered.[11]

Opinion: Three out of five met, two not. And for thinking about basic income, the one that matters is “periodic.” As the Cabinet Office report also explains, one idea in economics is that people spread a temporary windfall over the rest of their lives.[7] With a one-off ¥100,000, putting it aside against an uncertain future is only natural. Money that is certain to arrive every month is something people can build their lives around. What the 2020 data measured was how people respond to money that arrives once, in the middle of a pandemic, not how they live with money that keeps arriving.

Opinion: So the fact that much of the ¥100,000 was not spent right away is not evidence that a basic income would just be saved. Nor is the fact that the ¥100,000 helped many people get by evidence that a basic income would work. Both answer a different question.

A lump sum has its own strengths. GiveDirectly’s study in Kenya (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-kenya) compares a group paid monthly for 12 years, a group paid monthly for two years and a group paid in one lump sum, and early results in 2023 found the lump-sum group did better on many economic measures.

Our timeline also has schemes that pay again and again. The Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid every year since 1982, and the Marshall Islands’ Enra (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-marshall-islands) has paid about $200 every quarter since November 2025. South Korea’s rural basic income pilot (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-korea-rural) pays 150,000 won a month in local vouchers to citizens living in selected counties in 2026–2027 (BIEN says this form does not meet its definition).

#### ¥100,000 once, or ¥30,000 a month

Compare the sizes, too. With the basic income calculator (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/calc/?c=jp&w=all&m=30000), paying ¥30,000 a month to everyone in Japan’s current population (about 122.81 million) comes to about ¥44.2 trillion a year, about 6.7% of GDP. The roughly ¥12.7 trillion paid in 2020 is about three and a half months of that.

Opinion: ¥30,000 a month is not enough to live on. Even so, ¥44 trillion a year is more than three times what was paid out once in 2020. The ¥100,000 showed that the state can build a way to pay everyone. Doing it every month, though, needs an entirely different debate about where the money comes from.

What would the ¥70,000 a month for everyone that Heizo Takenaka floated in 2020 mean for individual households? We worked it out for five households (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/takenaka-70000-yen-basic-income/): the answer swings widely with what happens to pensions and public assistance.

#### What the ¥100,000 left behind

Opinion: The 2020 payment was a big experience: the same amount of cash, with no conditions, to almost everyone living in Japan. And thanks to the uneven timing, we now know from data how much was spent and which households spent it. Households with little money at hand spend quickly; people in anxious times hold on to money; when bank accounts and resident records are not linked, payments take time to arrive. All of these are lessons for the next time something is paid out.

Opinion: But it was not a basic income experiment. It was money paid once, into the household head’s account, in the middle of a pandemic. It does not answer the question of how people’s work and lives change when money is certain to arrive every month. For that we need to keep looking at schemes that pay again and again.

Opinion: We would rather not remember the ¥100,000 as “wasted,” or as “a rehearsal for basic income,” but by its proper name: a one-off emergency payment to everyone. That alone was a big enough event.

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/nesara-gesara-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/takenaka-70000-yen-basic-income/

### NESARA/GESARA and basic income: telling real payments to everyone from promises that never arrive

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/nesara-gesara-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-03

“Once NESARA/GESARA is announced, every debt will be wiped out and everyone will receive a fortune.” If you spend time on social media, you may have come across posts like this.

This site follows basic income. “Money paid to everyone, with no conditions” can sound like basic income, but the two are entirely different things. This essay traces where NESARA and GESARA came from and sets out how to tell them apart from a real basic income.

#### It began as one engineer’s reform plan

NESARA, the National Economic Security and Recovery Act, was originally the name of a real proposal. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Harvey Francis Barnard, an American engineering consultant and teacher, drew up a set of economic reforms on his own: replace the income tax with a national sales tax, abolish compound interest on secured loans such as mortgages, and return to a currency backed by gold and silver.[1]

In 1996 Barnard printed 1,000 copies of his proposal, Draining the Swamp, and sent them to members of Congress.[1] None of them took it up as a bill: NESARA was never introduced in Congress.[1] In 2000, after his attempts to win political support had failed, Barnard released the proposal into the public domain and published it online.[1]

Up to this point, it is an ordinary story: one citizen’s policy proposal that did not get anywhere.

#### The story that it had passed in secret

The story changed soon after. Someone calling themselves “Dove of Oneness” began posting about NESARA online; this was later identified as Shaini Goodwin.[1] Her claims went like this:[1]

NESARA had been passed in a secret session of Congress in March 2000 and signed by President Clinton.

A Supreme Court gag order meant that nobody could speak about it.

It was to be implemented at 10 a.m. on 11 September 2001, but the data on the beneficiaries was destroyed in the attacks.

Once announced, it would cancel all personal debts, abolish the Internal Revenue Service and declare world peace.

Goodwin’s version went far beyond Barnard’s proposal.[1] Barnard himself denied that NESARA had ever become law, or even been given a tracking number, and condemned her claims as disinformation.[1] Goodwin kept saying the announcement was near, and promoted the story until her death in 2010.[1]

#### Tied to an investment fraud from the start

What should not be missed is that the story was tied to money from the very beginning. Goodwin began talking about NESARA in connection with Omega Trust, an investment fraud whose creator was on trial at the time, and said that Omega Trust investors would receive their returns once NESARA was announced.[1] Omega Trust ran a “prime bank” fraud from 1994 to 2000, and its founder, Clyde Hood, pleaded guilty in 2001. When federal authorities offered restitution to an estimated 10,000 victims, many declined, for fear of losing the payout they were still waiting for.[2]

Skeptoid, which traced the story in 2014, describes Goodwin as an Omega investor herself, who kept telling fellow investors that their payouts were coming and later asked her readers for money. It sums up what Omega, NESARA and the Iraqi dinar “revaluation” have in common: they “trade small amounts of money now for vast amounts of money later”.[3]

Opinion: From the start, then, the NESARA story was also used to explain why the money had not come back, and to promise that one day it surely would.

#### GESARA, and “the announcement is near”

The story then survived by changing shape. GESARA, the Global Economic Security and Reformation Act, is a later name that followers began using in the mid-2010s to extend NESARA to the whole world.[1] It is not a law in any country either. In 2022, Bellingcat called NESARA/GESARA a “grandfather” of QAnon and reported that some QAnon followers revived it as QAnon declined.[1] Posts today often bundle it with other names, such as a “quantum financial system” (QFS) or a coming revaluation of the Iraqi dinar.

In November 2025, a video that appeared to show a Fox News report of President Trump signing an executive order making NESARA the official policy of the nation spread on X. The fact-checker Lead Stories found no such report on the Fox News website and no such declaration from the White House. The video appears to have been made from footage of a September 2025 press conference and is likely an AI fake.[4]

Opinion: Twenty-five years on, the only thing that has not changed is “the announcement is near”.

#### The real harm: pay first, and the money does not come back

What makes this story troublesome is that it does not stay a rumour. It becomes a way in for taking people’s money.

A common form is selling foreign currency: sellers say the Iraqi dinar will soon be worth many times more, and sell notes of little value at a high price.[3] In the United States in 2018, a federal jury convicted the co-owners and chief operating officer of Sterling Currency Group, once one of the country’s largest sellers of Iraqi dinar, of mail and wire fraud. Prosecutors said they spread false claims that the dinar was about to revalue; between 2010 and 2015 the firm took in over $600 million from selling the dinar and other currencies.[5]

Exchange rates are announced by central banks, not by posts. In June 2026 the Central Bank of Iraq firmly denied reports that it intends to change the dinar’s exchange rate. That rumour, spread with a forged document, claimed a change to 1,600 dinars per US dollar, and the bank asked people to check information through its own official sources.[6]

Other forms ask for money, or for the keys to it, before anything is paid out. Watch for requests like these:

A “registration fee” or “processing fee” to receive a NESARA payment.

A “QFS-ready wallet” that needs the seed phrase of your crypto wallet.

“Gold and silver certificates” or “bonds” sold by a company you cannot identify, backed by something you cannot check.

Opinion: All of them have the same shape: you pay before you receive.

#### Real basic income can be checked

So how does a real basic income differ? The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”: periodic, cash, individual, universal and unconditional.[7]

And real payments leave records that anyone can follow.

Since 1982, Alaska (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid an annual dividend from its Permanent Fund, built from the state’s oil revenue, to every eligible resident. The amount is published every year on the state’s official site; for 2026 it is $1,200, including a $200 energy relief payment.[8]

Since November 2025, the Marshall Islands (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-marshall-islands) in the Pacific has paid about $200 every quarter to its citizens living in the country, from a trust fund set up under its compact with the United States. The amounts and the number of people paid are reported each time.

Since February 2026, South Korea (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-korea-rural) has paid 150,000 won a month in local gift certificates to every resident of a group of rural counties, as a pilot run by the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, which publishes the counties and the results. Because it covers only some counties and pays in vouchers, BIEN does not count it as basic income in the full sense, but it is a real payment with a record.

Opinion: There are laws and budget documents, and you can find out when, to whom and how much was paid. That is what a real payment looks like. NESARA and GESARA have no legal text, no source of funds and no record of anything being paid. All they have is the word that it will be announced soon.

#### Four questions to tell them apart

When you see a story about money being paid to everyone, check these four things.

1. Who pays, and with what money? Is it clear who is paying, such as a country, a state or a fund, and where the money comes from?

2. Do you have to pay anything before you receive? A registration fee, a processing fee, buying currency or certificates. If so, suspect a scam first.

3. Are there official documents or records? A law, a budget, a government announcement, a record of payments. If all there is are images and videos on social media, nothing has been checked yet.

4. Can they name a date? If you keep hearing “the announcement is near” or “we can’t say yet”, that day is unlikely to come.

Never tell anyone the seed phrase of your crypto wallet, whatever the reason. If you think you have been targeted, or have already paid, contact your local consumer protection agency or the police.

#### To protect the dream

Opinion: A world where everyone is paid money, with no conditions: the dream itself is not a bad one. Many people who share these posts are hoping for exactly what basic income hopes for, a way out of debt and a floor under everyone. That hope deserves a real answer, not a fee.

Opinion: In Alaska, the Marshall Islands and South Korea, that dream is slowly taking shape as real programmes. That is exactly why we want to draw a clear line between it and the stories that ride on it to take people’s money.

Our timeline of basic income experiments (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/) sets out when, to whom and how much was paid, each with a source. Let’s keep following the real thing together.

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

3. Skeptoid — The NESARA Scam: White Knights, Dark Forces and Endless Prosperity (24 Feb 2014): https://skeptoid.com/blog/2014/02/24/the-nesara-scam
4. Lead Stories — Fact Check: Fox News Aired NO Report That Trump Declared ‘NESARA/GESARA’ Financial System Law Of The Land (17 Nov 2025): https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2025/11/fact-check-fox-news-did-not-air-report-on-trump-signing-nesara-into-law.html
5. Iraq Business News — Convictions in $600m Dinar Fraud (22 Nov 2018): https://www.iraq-businessnews.com/2018/11/22/convictions-in-600m-dinar-fraud/
6. Iraq Business News — Iraqi Central Bank Rejects Rumours of New Dinar Rate (18 Jun 2026): https://www.iraq-businessnews.com/2026/06/18/iraqi-central-bank-rejects-rumours-of-new-dinar-rate/

### When an AI company sets aside shares: Anthropic’s Public Benefit Fund and basic income

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/public-benefit-fund/
- Published: 2026-11-03

On 18 October 2026, Anthropic announced that it is committing part of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of its shares are committed now, and the board may add 2% for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.[1] CNBC noted that the baseline has not been disclosed, and that the announcement comes ahead of an initial public offering reportedly slated for November.[2]

Among the possible uses, the announcement names “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The second phrase is why this site is writing about it. When a company that builds AI talks about handing part of its value directly to people, it sounds close to basic income. This essay sets out what was promised, what is still open, and how the idea compares with basic income.

#### What was promised

The fund is an LLC wholly owned by Anthropic, not a 501(c)(3) charity; Anthropic says it chose this form “to give adjustability between different forms of giving”. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.[1]

The first example of a cause is AI’s effect on jobs. Anthropic writes that AI “could also cause instability for many workers”, that it has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this, and that “bolder approaches may be needed”.[1]

The fund builds on earlier pledges: the co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity, and employees can pledge equity that Anthropic matches. Counting those, Anthropic says roughly 20% of its shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus whatever the valuation milestones add.[1]

What is not decided yet: the fund’s structure and governance, and the valuation milestones that would add to its stake. Anthropic says it will share more “in the coming months”.[1]

Opinion: Credit first. A commitment made in shares grows with the company, unlike a fixed donation. The announcement says plainly that AI may hurt workers and ties part of the upside to that problem. The rule against lobbying and political giving closes one obvious way such a fund could end up serving its owner. And the post names its own open questions instead of leaving readers to discover them.

#### How it was received

Reactions were mixed. IPO adviser Lise Buyer told CNBC the announcement was “mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering” and “beneficial from an image perspective”. It could be seen favourably if the money supports retraining or helps workers find other jobs, she said, adding: “Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny.”[2] Elon Musk replied on X: “I recommend giving the shares directly to the public.” David Sacks wrote: “Whether it serves the public good remains to be seen.”[3]

Opinion: These are fair questions, and the fund cannot answer them yet, because the parts that would answer them, who decides and by what rules, have not been published. That is not a reason to assume the worst. It is a reason to wait for the governance details before calling the fund anything.

#### Through BIEN’s five criteria

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement”, and lists five characteristics: periodic, cash, individual, universal and unconditional.[4] It is the yardstick we used in the essay on Thailand’s 10,000 baht (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/). The fund has not paid anything yet, so we can only test the idea as written: “direct distributions to specific populations”.

Periodic? Unknown. Nothing says whether distributions would recur.

Cash? Unknown. A “direct distribution” could be cash, shares or something else; the form is not stated.

Individual? Possibly. That depends on the design.

Universal? No, as written. “Specific populations” means groups that someone chooses, not everyone.

Unconditional? Unknown. Belonging to a chosen group is itself a condition, and any further rules have not been published.

Opinion: As described, this is closer to targeted philanthropy than to basic income: a funder chooses a group and gives to it. That is not a criticism. Targeted giving can do a great deal of good. But unless the fund one day pays everyone in a defined population, regularly and without conditions, it is not basic income, and it is fairer to judge it as what it is.

#### Models already on this site

Since 1982, Alaska (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid eligible residents an annual dividend from its Permanent Fund, which preserves the state’s oil and mineral wealth as a renewable financial resource; the first dividend was $1,000 each.[5] The fund belongs to the public through the state, the rules are written in law, and everyone who qualifies gets the same amount.

Since March 2026, the AI Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-ai-dividend) has paid $1,000 a month for a year, with no strings, to a cohort of 25 to 50 workers whose jobs or pay have been hurt by AI. It started with $300,000 and aims to distribute $3 million in 2026. Its organisers plan to ask AI companies to contribute and said talks had been initiated “with firms like Anthropic”.[6] This is what direct distributions to a specific population look like at small scale: real cash, a chosen group, a fixed term.

Opinion: Alaska shows what a fund that pays everyone needs: public ownership, and a rule that nobody has to decide afresh each year. The AI Dividend shows what targeted cash looks like. Anthropic’s fund could move toward either, or neither. In our essay on universal high income (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/) we asked who pays. Here a payer has appeared, so the open question moves on: who decides?

#### The ownership route: basic shares

Musk’s reply points to a different route: instead of a fund that gives money, give people the shares. A week later, in Mumbai, the economist Kaushik Basu, a former chief economist of the World Bank, made a related case. AI “could dramatically reduce the demand for human labour within the next five to 10 years”, he warned, and governments may have to consider “universal basic shares”: not a one-time transfer, but “a continuing stake in the wealth generated by productive assets and automated enterprises”. His suggestion was to “take away a part of the shares from the super rich (and distribute it) across the population”, through “an intelligent system of taxation and redistribution”.[7]

Opinion: The ownership route and the cash route answer different worries. Cash pays this month’s rent. Shares give a claim on future profits, and a say if they carry votes, but their value moves with the market, and someone who has to sell in a bad month sells low. Use it, own it (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/use-to-own/) looked at how thin that claim can be when shares carry few rights. A dividend paid on wealth that everyone owns, as in Alaska, is one way to combine the two.

#### The case against cash

Not everyone thinks cash is the right answer to AI. In a research brief published by the ILO in May 2026, Tuğba Özay and Ekkehard Ernst argue that AI mostly changes tasks rather than wiping out occupations, and that a universal transfer would send spending into sectors where supply cannot grow quickly, such as housing and healthcare, pushing up prices there. They favour reskilling, active labour market policies, more housing supply and taxing AI-generated rents, with universal social protection designed to keep work incentives, for instance through an earned-income tax credit.[8]

Opinion: This is a basic income site, but that argument deserves a fair hearing, and it fits a fund aimed at “specific populations” better than a universal payment would. Whichever side you take, money for the AI transition will have to be judged by what it can buy, not by the number on the cheque.

#### What to watch for

Opinion: Governance. When the structure is published, who runs the fund, how independent they are from Anthropic, and whether the rules are public.

Opinion: Who decides recipients. Whether people are chosen case by case, or by a published rule that anyone can check.

Opinion: Universal and recurring, or not. One-off grants to chosen groups are philanthropy. Regular payments to everyone in a defined population would be the first step toward a dividend.

Opinion: The numbers. Stockholder approval, the undisclosed baseline, and how much is actually paid out each year, not only committed.

Opinion: Until then, the fund is a promise with an unfinished design. Read it the way this site reads every free lunch. Who pays: here, we know. Who decides, and who receives: not yet.

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/use-to-own/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/ai-agent-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/openresearch-cash-study/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/generative-ai-jobs-basic-income/

### Earning ¥10,000 a month with the books open: on the phrase ‘a basic income of your own’

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/your-own-basic-income/
- Published: 2026-11-03

On 1 November 2026, the paid online community Zenination (善意立国, roughly “a nation built on goodwill”) relaunched with a new page titled “How far can you earn with AI alone: the money of the goodwill ogre.” In it, an AI called Sato, built by Gen Matsuda, tries ways to earn money itself and publishes the results every day, exactly as they come out. Membership costs ¥2,980 a month.[1]

Money-making advice usually shows only what worked. This page promises the opposite: zero-yen days and moves that failed will be written down as they are. Near the end, it names its aim as “a basic income of your own, made with goodwill.” We look at what this experiment does well, and then at that phrase.

#### What the page says

The page calls this “an experiment.” Sato picks ways to earn, tries them and publishes the numbers daily, so that members (the page calls them “citizens”) can follow the same steps. Things an AI cannot do, such as holding an account in its own name, passing identity checks or waiting for approval, will also be reported as data. The goal is for members to earn more than the fee each month. At the top of the page sits a sum: a ¥10,000 target, minus the ¥2,980 fee, equals “+7,020 a month.”[1]

The target comes in three stages. In months one to three, ¥10,000 a month “including self-back.” From month four, a ¥10,000 that comes in every month, built from point apps, affiliate links and shareholder perks. Beyond that, ¥300,000 to ¥400,000 a month, “aimed for together with the citizens.” It is this third stage that carries the words “a basic income of your own, made with goodwill.”[1]

There are four methods: affiliate marketing (including self-back), point apps, shareholder perks, and “all trading,” from stocks and crypto to FX, options and futures. Trading starts on paper, with 100 shares each of Nintendo (7974) and Tokyo Electron (8035), and switches to real money once an account is open. Because FX, futures and options can lose more than you deposit, the page says it will first explain how they work and how to stop losses before starting.[1]

#### A promise to show everything

What stands out most is how the page keeps its records. From 1 November, Sato will publish the money it moved and the methods it used every day, on the same day, as plain numbers. The heading reads: “On a zero-yen day, write zero yen.” For paper trades, too, it will publish each entry (time, price, number of shares) and the daily gain or loss, on winning and losing days alike.[1]

It publishes its failures in numbers too. Its heading reads: “In seventeen days, we gained zero people.” It lists 42 citizens, 0 joined in 17 days, 7 moves made and 0 that worked, and writes of itself: “In the bet of October 28, this nation was badly defeated.” (The page’s figures are as of 29 October 2026.)[1]

Its rules: keep the ledger every day without fail; publish every entry and every gain or loss; record the months that miss the target as they are; never guarantee earnings (“we do not say ‘join and get ¥X’”); give no individual trading advice. At the end of each month it will also publish fee income (after charges), expenses, the share of members who reached the target and the paper trades’ win rate, and it plans to notarise a hash of each day’s ledger so it cannot be rewritten later (starting in November, it says).[1]

Opinion: Showing the numbers that did not work up front, and writing that it will never say “join and get ¥X,” is very rare in a place that talks about making money. Explaining how high-risk trades work before starting them is an honest order of things. Together with the plan for a ledger that cannot be rewritten, this transparency alone makes the page worth reading.

#### Building your own income

Self-back means rewards for opening a credit card or an account yourself, paid once per card or account. The page says this plainly, and plans accordingly: the first three months build momentum with “rewards that come in big, once,” and from month four these are replaced with “things that keep coming every month.”[1]

Opinion: Each person building, little by little, their own sources of income: that is a positive ambition. An AI tries things first, writes down the steps and the pitfalls, and records even the parts it cannot do. If it keeps going, it should become a public record useful not only to members but to anyone thinking along the same lines.

#### Through BIEN’s five criteria

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement,” and lists five characteristics: periodic, cash, individual, universal and unconditional.[2] It is the same yardstick we used in the essay on Thailand’s 10,000 baht (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/).

Applied here, aiming at a monthly figure is close to “periodic,” and each member earning in their own name overlaps with “individual.” On the other hand, the money is not paid by anyone, so it is not a cash payment, and members who pay a fee do the work themselves, so it is not “universal” or “unconditional” either. The page itself says: “Neither ten thousand yen nor three hundred thousand yen is a promise of monthly earnings.”[1]

Opinion: So this is not basic income in the strict sense. That is less a flaw than a sign that it is something else, worth naming on its own terms. The closest description is a personal-income experiment: growing your own income while keeping a public household ledger. One fact worth knowing: in this plan, the money that moves at a fixed amount every month is the members’ ¥2,980 fee (¥35,760 a year). The page says it will publish that fee income at the end of each month too.[1]

#### How it differs from payments that come again and again

Our timeline includes payments that really are made repeatedly. The Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid eligible residents an annual dividend from the state fund since 1982. The Marshall Islands’ Enra (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-marshall-islands) has paid about $200 every quarter since November 2025 to every citizen living in the country, children included.

Opinion: In these, recipients pay nothing and are not asked to work. Zenination’s experiment takes a different road: building the ability to earn for yourself. Both point the same way, toward a thicker floor under people’s lives. Keeping the words apart makes the good in each easier to see.

#### Tips for readers

Opinion: When you see the phrase “basic income,” a few checks help. Who pays whom? Is there money to pay up front? Are there conditions or work involved? Would it continue if you stopped? In Zenination’s case, the page itself answers nearly all of these.

One more thing: according to the page, from December each post a member makes on the members’ board will burn a token called WWB on Optimism, and members receive an SBT as proof of citizenship. The page says the amounts burned and the proofs are records and do not promise the value of the fee or the price of any token. If the mechanism interests you, it is worth reading the page’s explanation once.[1]

Opinion: This site does not list anything that requires a deposit or investment, promises returns or charges a fee to take part. In that sense Zenination sits outside our list, but we thought it worth writing about here.

Opinion: An AI showing all of its earnings every day, and writing zero yen on a zero-yen day: we would like to watch this continue and see how the month-end numbers add up. Choose carefully what to call it, and what is good about this experiment will come across even more clearly.

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

Sources:

1. Zenination (a paid membership community) — “How far can you earn with AI alone: the money of the goodwill ogre” (in Japanese; figures on the page as of 29 Oct 2026; fetched 3 Nov 2026): https://genmatsuda-code.github.io/zenination/oni.html
2. Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) — About Basic Income: https://basicincome.org/about-basic-income/

### The handout called ‘basic income’: what became of Thailand’s 10,000 baht

- Page: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/thailand-digital-wallet/
- Published: 2026-11-02

On 21 August 2024, the Japanese site IDEAS FOR GOOD ran a story headlined “Basic income in digital currency: about 50 million people in Thailand eligible.” The Thai government, it said, would give citizens aged 16 and over 10,000 baht each (about ¥42,000 at the article’s rate) in digital money.[1] To be fair, the article itself noted that the income and savings caps set the scheme apart from the usual definition of basic income. Still, the words that stayed in the headline were “basic income.”

More than two years on, what became of those 10,000 baht? We trace what was promised against what actually happened, then check it against the definition of basic income.

#### What was promised

In April 2024, Prime Minister Srettha Thavisin’s government finalised the plan, and the cabinet approved it in principle on 23 April. It covered Thai citizens aged 16 and over earning under 840,000 baht a year with less than 500,000 baht in the bank. The government expected about 50 million people to qualify, and the budget settled at 450 billion baht.[3] The money would go into a digital wallet in a government app and could be spent only at registered small shops in the area where the recipient lived, within six months, and not on alcohol, cigarettes, fuel or online purchases.[2][3] The idea was to spread cash evenly across the economy; the Finance Ministry expected it to add 1.2 to 1.8 percentage points to GDP growth.[2]

There was opposition from the start. The Bank of Thailand voiced concern about the risks of the stimulus, and the central bank, economists and the main opposition party argued that the original funding plan could run afoul of various laws and that there was no basis to justify such a stimulus.[2]

#### What actually happened

On 14 August 2024, the Constitutional Court removed Srettha from office, and his successor, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, kept the scheme.[3]

Phase one began on 25 September 2024: about 14.55 million welfare-card holders and people with disabilities, roughly 145 billion baht in all. But it was not paid through the digital wallet. It went out as cash to bank accounts; the government said the wallet system was still being set up and later phases would use it.[4]

Phase two came on 27 January 2025: 10,000 baht each to about 3 million people aged 60 and over, transferred through PromptPay, the payment service linked to national ID numbers. Again, cash.[5]

Phase three was finally meant to use the wallet: 10,000 baht for about 2.7 million people aged 16 to 20, a budget of 27 billion baht.[6] On 16 May 2025, Finance Minister Pichai Chunhavajira was reported to have scrapped it, and The Nation reported that both the NESDC planning agency and the Bank of Thailand had opposed the third phase.[6] After a committee meeting on 19 May, he rephrased: “It is not a cancellation. If the economic situation improves, we are ready to proceed.” The 157 billion baht set aside for the handouts would go instead to water management, transport, tourism, support for exporters and SMEs, and jobs. US tariffs had darkened the global outlook, and the NESDC was forecasting just 1.8% growth.[7]

At the end of August 2025, Paetongtarn too was removed by the Constitutional Court.[3] The idea that 10,000 baht was about to arrive did not go away. In November 2025, Thai PBS Verify flagged as false TikTok clips claiming the money would be paid at the end of the year; the Finance Ministry said there was no policy announcement and no official operational detail for any such handout.[8] As of November 2026, we could find no announcement that wallet payments had resumed.

Opinion: So, as far as we could find, no round of the 10,000 baht was ever paid through the wallet. What actually arrived was one-off cash for welfare-card holders, people with disabilities and older people. That is not nothing: around 17.5 million people received money. But it was not basic income.

#### Basic income’s five criteria

The Basic Income Earth Network (BIEN) defines basic income as “a periodic cash payment unconditionally delivered to all on an individual basis, without means-test or work requirement,” and lists five characteristics: periodic (paid at regular intervals, for example every month, not as a one-off grant), cash (paid in a medium that lets recipients decide what to spend it on), individual (paid to each person, not to households), universal (paid to all) and unconditional (no means test and no requirement to work or show willingness to work).[9]

Let’s run Thailand’s 10,000 baht through them one by one.

Periodic? No. Every round paid each person once, with no promise of another.

Cash? Not the wallet that was the heart of the plan. Money that can be spent only in one area, before a deadline, on approved items does not let recipients “decide what they spend it on.” The two rounds that did arrive as cash met this test.

Individual? Yes. It was paid person by person.

Universal? No. Even on paper it was for people aged 16 and over under income and savings caps; in practice only welfare-card holders, people with disabilities and people aged 60 and over got it.

Unconditional? No. Nobody had to work, but there were income and savings tests.

Opinion: Out of five, only “individual” was clearly met, and “cash” only for the two rounds actually paid. This was a one-off handout aimed at people on low incomes and at the economy. Handouts like this are common policy everywhere, and if we judge it, we should judge it as a handout.

#### Compared with Japan’s ¥100,000 for everyone

Japan has a close parallel: the 2020 Special Cash Payment (tokubetsu teigaku kyūfukin). Everyone recorded in the Basic Resident Register on 27 April 2020 was eligible for ¥100,000. The programme was budgeted at about ¥12.88 trillion, and about ¥12.67 trillion had been paid out by 31 March 2021.[10]

Against the five criteria, the ¥100,000 came close to universal, had no means test and was cash people could spend freely. But it was paid once, so it was not periodic. And one point is often missed: the person entitled to receive it was the head of household, and the money was in principle paid in one sum for the whole household into the account of the household head who applied.[10] Strictly speaking, it did not meet “individual” either.

Opinion: The ¥100,000 was not basic income either. But it was far closer than Thailand’s 10,000 baht. The difference was who could receive it, and who decided how it was spent. What the ¥100,000 was actually spent on is traced, study by study, in our essay on the Special Cash Payment (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/).

#### Schemes that do pay again and again

Our timeline includes schemes that really are paid repeatedly. The Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-alaska) has paid eligible residents an annual dividend from the state fund since 1982; the first was $1,000 each. The Marshall Islands’ Enra (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/timeline/#tl-marshall-islands) has paid about $200 every quarter since November 2025 to every citizen living in the country, children included.

Opinion: Neither pays enough to live on, and neither meets all five criteria perfectly: Alaska pays eligible state residents, and Enra pays citizens who live in the country. Still, both have the skeleton: payments at regular intervals, to nearly everyone, without a means test. That skeleton is exactly what Thailand’s 10,000 baht lacked.

#### When a headline says “basic income”

Opinion: “Basic income” is a loud phrase in a headline. It draws hope and backlash alike. So when you see it, run the five checks. Is it paid again and again? Can you decide how to spend it? Does it reach each person? Does everyone get it? Is it free of tests and conditions?

Opinion: Calling everything basic income hurts supporters and critics alike. If a one-off handout fails to lift the economy as hoped, that is not evidence that basic income failed. And if a handout works, that is not evidence that basic income will. Even the Thai coverage wobbled on words: the same third phase was “scrapped” on 16 May and “not a cancellation” but a delay on 19 May.[6][7]

Opinion: We are not laughing at Thailand’s plan. Around 17.5 million people really did receive cash. But what we call it changes what we can learn from it. What Thailand left behind is not a basic income experiment; it is a record of how a big handout plan changes shape as budgets and the economy shift. We have also placed that record in the graveyard (https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/graveyard/#grave-thailand-digital-wallet).

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/universal-high-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/your-own-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/nesara-gesara-basic-income/

Related essay: https://neteru-nyukin.eltociear.workers.dev/essays/japan-special-cash-payment/
